user_input: What's the recommended way to target a button by the label a user would read on it?
reference: Reach for a role locator such as page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }). Playwright pushes you toward role-based locators because they mirror how real users and assistive tech experience the page.
reference_contexts: We recommend prioritizing role locators to locate elements, as it is the closest way to how users and assistive technology perceive the page.
llm_response:
To target a button by the label a user would read on it, the documentation recommends using **`page.getByRole()`** with the `button` role and the `name` option. This approach is preferred because it reflects how users and assistive technology perceive the page.

**Recommended approach:**
```javascript
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
```

**Alternative approach:**
While `page.getByLabel()` is available, the documentation specifies that it is intended for locating **form controls** (such as inputs, checkboxes, or radio buttons) by their associated label text or `aria-label` attributes. It is not the recommended method for targeting buttons.

Playwright can interact with HTML Input elements such as text inputs, checkboxes, radio buttons, select options, mouse clicks, type characters, keys and shortcuts as well as upload files and focus elements.

## Text input​ {#text-input}

Using
locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill)
is the easiest way to fill out the form fields. It focuses the element and triggers an
`input`
event with the entered text. It works for
`<input>`
,
`<textarea>`
and
`[contenteditable]`
elements.


`// Text inputawaitpage.getByRole

## Checkboxes and radio buttons​ {#checkboxes-and-radio-buttons}

Using
locator.setChecked() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-checked)
is the easiest way to check and uncheck a checkbox or a radio button. This method can be used with
`input[type=checkbox]`
,

and

elements.

## Select options​ {#select-options}

Selects one or multiple options in the

. You can specify option

## Mouse click​ {#mouse-click}

Performs a simple human click.


`// Generic clickawaitpage.getByRole('button').click();// Double clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').dblclick();// Right clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({button:'right'});// Shift + clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['Shift']});// Ctrl + click on Windows and Linux// Meta + click on macOSawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['ControlOrMeta']});// Hover over elementawaitpage.getByText('Item').hover();// Click the top left cornerawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({position:{x:0,y:0}});`


Under the hood, this and other pointer-related methods:

wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
wait for it to become displayed, i.e. not empty, no
`display:none`
, no
`visibility:hidden`
wait for it to stop moving, for example, until css transition finishes
scroll the element into view
wait for it to receive pointer events at the action point, for example, waits until element becomes non-obscured by other elements
retry if the element is detached during any of the above checks

#### Forcing the click​ {#forcing-the

-click}

Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the
actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
checks and force the click:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click({force:true});`

HTMLElement.click() (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/click)
behavior via simply dispatching a click event on the element with
locator.dispatchEvent() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-dispatch-event)
:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');`

Playwright can interact with HTML Input elements such as text inputs, checkboxes, radio buttons, select options, mouse clicks, type characters, keys and shortcuts as well as upload files and focus elements.

## Text input​ {#text-input}

Using
locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill)
is the easiest way to fill out the form fields. It focuses the element and triggers an
`input`
event with the entered text. It works for
`<input>`
,
`<textarea>`
and
`[contenteditable]`
elements.


`// Text inputawaitpage.getByRole

## Checkboxes and radio buttons​ {#checkboxes-and-radio-buttons}

Using
locator.setChecked() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-checked)
is the easiest way to check and uncheck a checkbox or a radio button. This method can be used with

,
`input[type=radio]`
and

elements.


`// Check the checkboxawaitpage.getByLabel('I agree to the terms above').check();// Assert the checked stateexpect(page.getByLabel('Subscribe to newsletter')).toBeChecked();// Select the radio buttonawaitpage.getByLabel('XL').check();`


## Select options​ {#select-options}

`<select>`
element with

. You can specify option
`value`
, or
`label`
to select. Multiple options can be selected.

## Mouse click​ {#mouse-click}

Performs a simple human click.


`// Generic clickawaitpage.getByRole('button').click();// Double clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').dblclick();// Right clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({button:'right'});// Shift + clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['Shift']});// Ctrl + click on Windows and Linux// Meta + click on macOSawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['ControlOrMeta']});// Hover over elementawaitpage.getByText('Item').hover();// Click the top left cornerawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({position:{x:0,y:0}});`


Under the hood, this and other pointer-related methods:

wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
wait for it to become displayed, i.e. not empty, no
`display:none`
, no
`visibility:hidden`
wait for it to stop moving, for example, until css transition finishes
scroll the element into view
wait for it to receive pointer events at the action point, for example, waits until element becomes non-obscured by other elements
retry if the element is detached during any of the above checks

#### Forcing the click​ {#forcing-the
160|-click}

Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the
actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
checks and force the click:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click({force:true});`


#### Programmatic click​ {#programmatic-click}

If you are not interested in testing your app under the real conditions and want to simulate the click by any means possible, you can trigger the
HTMLElement.click() (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/click)
behavior via simply dispatching a click event on the element with
locator.dispatchEvent() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-dispatch-event)
:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');`

user_input: If I don't configure anything, how long can a single test run before Playwright kills it, and what counts toward that budget?
reference: Each test gets 30 seconds out of the box, and that budget covers the test body plus fixture setup and any beforeEach hooks.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
llm_response:
If you do not configure anything, Playwright enforces a default timeout of **30 seconds** for each test.

The following activities count toward this budget:
*   The test function itself.
*   Fixture setups.
*   `beforeEach` hooks.

Additionally, there is a separate timeout of the same value (30 seconds) shared between fixture teardowns and `afterEach` hooks. `beforeAll` and `afterAll` hooks also have a separate timeout equal to the test timeout, but they do not share time with any test.

`beforeEach`

Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

## Assertion testing vs Snapshot testing​ {#assertion-testing-vs-snapshot-testing}

Snapshot testing and assertion testing serve different purposes in test automation:

### Assertion testing​ {#assertion-testing}

Assertion testing is a targeted approach where you assert specific values or conditions about elements or components. For instance, with Playwright,
expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text)
verifies that an element contains the expected text, and
expect(locator).toHaveValue() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-value)
confirms that an input field has the expected value. Assertion tests are specific and generally check the current state of an element or property against an expected, predefined state. They work well for predictable, single-value checks but

are limited in scope when testing the broader structure or variations.

Advantages

Clarity
: The intent of the test is explicit and easy to understand.
Specificity
: Tests focus on particular aspects of functionality, making them more robust against unrelated changes.
Debugging
: Failures provide targeted feedback, pointing directly to the problematic aspect.

Disadvantages

Verbose for complex outputs
: Writing assertions for complex data structures or large outputs can be cumbersome and error-prone.
Maintenance overhead
: As code evolves, manually updating assertions can be time-consuming.

### Snapshot testing​ {#snapshot-testing}

Snapshot testing captures a “snapshot” or representation of the entire state of an element, component, or data at a given moment, which is then saved for future comparisons. When re-running tests, the current state is compared to the snapshot, and if there are differences, the test fails. This approach is especially useful for complex or dynamic structures, where manually asserting each detail would be too time-consuming. Snapshot testing is broader and more holistic than assertion testing, allowing you to track more complex changes over time.

Advantages

Simplifies complex outputs
: For example, testing a UI component's rendered output can be tedious with traditional assertions. Snapshots capture the entire output for easy comparison.
Quick Feedback loop
: Developers can easily spot unintended changes in the output.
Encourages consistency
: Helps maintain consistent output as code evolves.

Disadvantages

Over-Reliance
: It can be

tempting to accept changes to snapshots without fully understanding them, potentially hiding bugs.
Granularity
: Large snapshots may be hard to interpret when differences arise, especially if minor changes affect large portions of the output.
Suitability
: Not ideal for highly dynamic content where outputs change frequently or unpredictably.

### When to use​ {#when-to-use}

Snapshot testing
is ideal for:
UI testing of whole pages and components.
Broad structural checks for complex UI components.
Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure.
Assertion testing
is ideal for:
Core logic validation.
Computed value testing.
Fine-grained tests requiring precise conditions.

By combining snapshot testing for broad, structural checks and assertion testing for specific functionality, you can achieve a well-rounded testing strategy.

## Aria snapshots​ {#aria-snapshots}

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing
roles
,
attributes
,
values

For instance, with Playwright, expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) verifies that an element contains the expected text, and expect(locator).toHaveValue() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-value) confirms that an input field has the expected value. Assertion tests are specific and generally check the current state of an element or property against an expected, predefined state. They work well for predictable, single-value checks but 113| are limited in scope when testing the broader structure or variations. Advantages Clarity : The intent of the test is explicit and easy to understand. Specificity : Tests focus on particular aspects of functionality, making them more robust against unrelated changes. Debugging : Failures provide targeted feedback, pointing directly to the problematic aspect. Disadvantages Verbose for complex outputs : Writing assertions for complex data structures or large outputs can be cumbersome and error-prone. Maintenance overhead : As code evolves, manually updating assertions can be time-consuming. ### Snapshot testing​ {#snapshot-testing} Snapshot testing captures a “snapshot” or representation of the entire state of an element, component, or data at a given moment, which is then saved for future comparisons. When re-running tests, the current state is compared to the snapshot, and if there are differences, the test fails. This approach is especially useful for complex or dynamic structures, where manually asserting each detail would be too time-consuming. Snapshot testing is broader and more holistic than assertion testing, allowing you to track more complex changes over time. Advantages Simplifies complex outputs : For example, testing a UI component's rendered output can be tedious with traditional assertions. Snapshots capture the entire output for easy comparison. Quick Feedback loop : Developers can easily spot unintended changes in the output. Encourages consistency : Helps maintain consistent output as code evolves. Disadvantages Over-Reliance : It can be 113| tempting to accept changes to snapshots without fully understanding them, potentially hiding bugs. Granularity : Large snapshots may be hard to interpret when differences arise, especially if minor changes affect large portions of the output. Suitability : Not ideal for highly dynamic content where outputs change frequently or unpredictably. ### When to use​ {#when-to-use} Snapshot testing is ideal for: UI testing of whole pages and components. Broad structural checks for complex UI components. Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure. Assertion testing is ideal for: Core logic validation. Computed value testing. Fine-grained tests requiring precise conditions. By combining snapshot testing for broad, structural checks and assertion testing for specific functionality, you can achieve a well-rounded testing strategy. ## Aria snapshots​ {#aria-snapshots} In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles , attributes , values , and text content . user_input: I have a flaky test I'd like re-run a couple of times on failure — what's the quickest command-line way?
reference: Pass a retry count on the run command, e.g. npx playwright test --retries=3 re-runs failing tests up to three times. Nothing is retried unless you opt in.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.
llm_response:
The quickest command-line way to re-run failed tests is to use the `--retries` flag. You can specify the number of retry attempts by passing the desired number to this flag:

`npx playwright test --retries=N`

(Replace `N` with the number of times you want the test to be retried upon failure.)

are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

user_input: How do I grab a screenshot of the whole scrollable page rather than just the visible area?
reference: Flip on the fullPage flag when you screenshot the page: page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true }).
reference_contexts: await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true });
llm_response:
To capture a screenshot of the full scrollable page, you should use the `fullPage` option set to `true` within the `page.screenshot()` method.

**Example:**
```javascript
await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true });
```

The `fullPage` option is a boolean that, when true, captures the entire scrollable page instead of just the currently visible viewport. It defaults to `false`.

user_input: Can I screenshot a single element instead of the entire page?
reference: Yes — call .screenshot() directly on that element's locator, e.g. page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' }).
reference_contexts: await page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' });
llm_response:
Yes, you can screenshot a single element.

The recommended approach is to use **`locator.screenshot()`**, which captures a screenshot of the element matching the locator.

**Example usage:**
```javascript
await page.getByRole('link').screenshot({ path: 'link.png' });
```

**Alternative approaches:**
*   **`elementHandle.screenshot()`**: This is an older method that also captures a screenshot of a specific element. However, the documentation explicitly discourages its use in favor of `locator.screenshot()`.
*   **`page.screenshot()`**: While primarily for the entire page, it can be used to capture a specific element by calling it on a locator (e.g., `await page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' });`).

Both `locator.screenshot()` and `elementHandle.screenshot()` provide configuration options for animations, image quality, scale, style, timeout, and file type.

user_input: I pulled a trace.zip off CI — how do I actually open it on my machine?
reference: Hand it to the CLI: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip.
reference_contexts: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip
llm_response:
To open a `trace.zip` file on your machine, you can use one of the following methods:

### 1. Using the Playwright CLI (Recommended)
You can open the trace file directly from your terminal using the `show-trace` command:
```bash
npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip
```

### 2. Using the Web-based Trace Viewer
You can use the statically hosted version of the Trace Viewer at [trace.playwright.dev](https://trace.playwright.dev). 
*   Navigate to the website in your browser.
*   Drag and drop your `trace.zip` file onto the page, or use the **Select file** button to upload it.
*   The trace is processed locally in your browser and no data is transmitted externally.

### 3. Viewing via HTML Report
If you have an HTML report generated from your test run, you can open the report and click on the trace icon next to the test's file name to view the trace.

## Trace Viewer features​ {#trace-viewer-features}

### Actions​ {#actions}

In the Actions tab you can see what locator was used for every action and how long each one took to run. Hover over each action of your test and visually see the change in the DOM snapshot. Go back and forward in time and click an action to inspect and debug. Use the Before and After tabs to visually see what happened before and after the action.

Selecting each action reveals:

Action snapshots
Action log
Source code location

### Screens type of the action, it will capture:

Type
Description
Before
A snapshot at the time action is called.
Action
A snapshot at the moment of the performed input. This type of snapshot is especially useful when exploring where exactly Playwright clicked.
After
A snapshot after the action.

Here is what the typical Action snapshot looks like:

Notice how it highlights both, the DOM Node as well as the exact click position.

### Source​ {#source}

When you click on an action in the sidebar, the line of code for that action is highlighted in the source panel.

### Call​ {#call}

The call tab shows you information about the action such as the time it took, what locator was used, if in strict mode and

the request headers, response headers, request body and response body.

Double click on an action from your test in the actions sidebar. This will filter the network requests to only show the requests that were made during that action. Click the
Show all
button to see all network requests again.

Use the timeline to filter actions, by clicking a start point and dragging to an ending point. The network tab will also be filtered to only show the network requests that were made during the actions selected.

### Metadata​ {#metadata}

Next to the Actions tab you will find the Metadata tab which will show you more information on your test such as the Browser, viewport size, test duration and more.

### Attachments​ {#attachments}

The "Attachments" tab allows you to explore attachments. If you're doing
visual regression testing (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots)
, you'll be able to compare screenshots by examining the image diff, the actual image and the expected image. When you click on the expected image you can use the slider to slide one image over the other so you can easily see the differences in your screenshots.

### Actions​ {#actions}

In the Actions tab you can see what locator was used for every action and how long each one took to run. Hover over each action of your test and visually see the change in the DOM snapshot. Go back and forward in time and click an action to inspect and debug. Use the Before and After tabs to visually see what happened before and after the action.

Selecting each action reveals:

Action snapshots
Action log
Source code location

### Screens type of the action, it will capture:

Type
Description
Before
A snapshot at the time action is called.
Action
A snapshot at the moment of the performed input. This type of snapshot is especially useful when exploring where exactly Playwright clicked.
After
A snapshot after the action.

Here is what the typical Action snapshot looks like:

Notice how it highlights both, the DOM Node as well as the exact click position.

### Source​ {#source}

When you click on an action in the sidebar, the line of code for that action is highlighted in the source panel.

### Call​ {#call}

The call tab shows you information about the action such as the time it took, what locator was used, if in strict mode and
383| what key was used.

### Log​ {#log}

See a full log of your test to better understand what Playwright is doing behind the scenes such as scrolling into view, waiting for element to be visible, enabled and stable and performing actions such as click, fill, press etc.

### Errors​ {#errors}

If your test fails you will see the error messages for each test in the Errors tab. The timeline will also show a red line highlighting where the error occurred. You can also click on the source tab to see on which line of the source code the error is.

### Console​ {#console}

See console logs from the browser as well as from your test. Different icons are displayed to show you if the console log came from the browser or from the test file.

Double click on an action from your test in the actions sidebar. This will filter the console to only show the logs that were made during that action. Click the
Show all
button to see all console logs again.

Use the timeline to filter actions, by clicking a start point and dragging to an ending point. The console tab will also be filtered to only show the logs that were made during the actions selected.

### Network​ {#network}

The Network tab shows you all the network requests that were made during your test. You can sort by different types of requests, status code, method, request, content type, duration and size. Click on a request to see more information about it such as
383| the request headers, response headers, request body and response body.

Double click on an action from your test in the actions sidebar. This will filter the network requests to only show the requests that were made during that action. Click the
Show all
button to see all network requests again.

Use the timeline to filter actions, by clicking a start point and dragging to an ending point. The network tab will also be filtered to only show the network requests that were made during the actions selected.

### Metadata​ {#metadata}

Next to the Actions tab you will find the Metadata tab which will show you more information on your test such as the Browser, viewport size, test duration and more.

### Attachments​ {#attachments}

The "Attachments" tab allows you to explore attachments. If you're doing
visual regression testing (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots)
, you'll be able to compare screenshots by examining the image diff, the actual image and the expected image. When you click on the expected image you can use the slider to slide one image over the other so you can easily see the differences in your screenshots.

To cap the number of tests running in parallel from the command line, use the `--workers` flag followed by the desired number of worker processes.

`npx playwright test --workers=4`

`npx playwright test --workers=1`

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes

are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:


`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locallyworkers:process.env.CI?2:undefined,});`


## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`


## Parallelize tests in a single file​ {#parallelize-tests-in-a

-single-file}

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'parallel'});test('runs in parallel 1',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('runs in parallel 2',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


Alternatively, you can opt-in all tests into this fully-parallel mode in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({fullyParallel:true,});`


You can also opt in for fully-parallel mode for just a few projects:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// runs all tests in all files of a specific project in parallelprojects:[{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome']},fullyParallel:true,},]});`


## Serial mode​ {#serial-mode}

You can annotate inter-dependent tests

as serial. If one of the serial tests fails, all subsequent tests are skipped. All tests in a group are retried together.

note
Using serial is not recommended. It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be run independently.


`import{test,typePage}from'@playwright/test';// Annotate entire file as serial.test.describe.configure({mode:'serial'});letpage:Page;test.beforeAll(async({browser})=>{page=awaitbrowser.newPage();});test.afterAll(async()=>{awaitpage.close();});test('runs first',async()=>{awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev/');});test('runs second',async()=>{awaitpage.getByText('Get Started').click();});`


## Opt out of fully parallel mode​ {#opt-out-of-fully-parallel-mode}

If your configuration applies parallel mode to all tests using
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
, you might still want to run some tests with default settings. You can override the mode per describe:


`test.describe('runs in parallel with other describes',()=>{test.describe.configure({mode:'default'});test('in order 1',async({page})=>{});test('in order 2',async({page})=>{});});`

Your tests modify shared server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting.

When not to use

Your tests do not modify any shared server-side state. In this case, all tests can use a single shared account.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes
0| are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:


`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locallyworkers:process.env.CI?2:undefined,});`


## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`


## Parallelize tests in a single file​ {#parallelize-tests-in-a
0|-single-file}

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'parallel'});test('runs in parallel 1',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('runs in parallel 2',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


Alternatively, you can opt-in all tests into this fully-parallel mode in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({fullyParallel:true,});`


You can also opt in for fully-parallel mode for just a few projects:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// runs all tests in all files of a specific project in parallelprojects:[{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome']},fullyParallel:true,},]});`


## Serial mode​ {#serial-mode}

You can annotate inter-dependent tests
0| as serial. If one of the serial tests fails, all subsequent tests are skipped. All tests in a group are retried together.

note
Using serial is not recommended. It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be run independently.


`import{test,typePage}from'@playwright/test';// Annotate entire file as serial.test.describe.configure({mode:'serial'});letpage:Page;test.beforeAll(async({browser})=>{page=awaitbrowser.newPage();});test.afterAll(async()=>{awaitpage.close();});test('runs first',async()=>{awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev/');});test('runs second',async()=>{awaitpage.getByText('Get Started').click();});`


## Opt out of fully parallel mode​ {#opt-out-of-fully-parallel-mode}

If your configuration applies parallel mode to all tests using
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
, you might still want to run some tests with default settings. You can override the mode per describe:


`test.describe('runs in parallel with other describes',()=>{test.describe.configure({mode:'default'});test('in order 1',async({page})=>{});test('in order 2',async({page})=>{});});`

user_input: If my selector happens to match several elements and I try to click, what does Playwright do?
reference: It refuses to guess — locators are strict, so any action that needs one element throws when the locator resolves to more than one.
reference_contexts: Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:
llm_response:
When using a locator, Playwright supports a "strict mode" (which is often the default) to ensure a single target DOM element is matched. If your selector matches several elements, Playwright will throw an error.

To handle cases where multiple elements are matched, you have the following options:

*   **Explicitly select one element:** You can use `locator.first()`, `locator.last()`, or `locator.nth(index)` to specify which element to target.
*   **Perform a multiple-element operation:** Some methods, such as `locator.count()`, are designed to work with multiple elements and will not throw an error.
*   **Disable strict mode:** You can explicitly opt-out of the strictness check if necessary.

### Live editing locators​ {#live-editing-locators}

While running in debug mode you can live edit the locators. Next to the 'Pick Locator' button there is a field showing the
locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
that the test is paused on. You can edit this locator directly in the
Pick Locator
field, and matching elements will be highlighted in the browser window.

### Picking locators​ {#picking-locators}

While debugging, you might need to choose a more resilient locator. You can do this by clicking on the
Pick Locator
button and hovering over any element in the browser window. While hovering over an element you will see the code needed to locate this element highlighted below. Clicking an element in the browser will add the locator into the field where you can then either tweak it or copy it into your code.

Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing
role, text and test id locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
. If Playwright finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient and uniquely identify the target element, so you don't have to worry about failing tests due to locators.

### Actionability logs​ {#actionability-logs}

By the time Playwright has paused on a

click action, it has already performed
actionability checks (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
that can be found in the log. This can help you understand what happened during your test and what Playwright did or tried to do. The log tells you if the element was visible, enabled and stable, if the locator resolved to an element, scrolled into view, and so much more. If actionability can't be reached, it will show the action as pending.

#### Debug one test on a specific browser​ {#debug-one-test-on-a-specific-browser}

To run one test on a specific browser add the name of the test file and the line number of the test you want to debug as well as the
`--project through each action of your test using the toolbar at the top of the Inspector. You can see the current action highlighted in the test code, and matching elements highlighted in the browser window.

### Run a test from a specific breakpoint​ {#run-a-test-from-a-specific-breakpoint}

To speed up the debugging process you can add a
page.pause() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-pause)
method to your test. This way you won't have to step through each action of your test to get to the point where you want to debug.


`awaitpage.pause();`


Once you add a
`page.pause()`
call, run your tests in debug mode. Clicking the "Resume" button in
256| the Inspector will run the test and only stop on the
`page.pause()`
.

### Live editing locators​ {#live-editing-locators}

While running in debug mode you can live edit the locators. Next to the 'Pick Locator' button there is a field showing the
locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
that the test is paused on. You can edit this locator directly in the
Pick Locator
field, and matching elements will be highlighted in the browser window.

### Picking locators​ {#picking-locators}

While debugging, you might need to choose a more resilient locator. You can do this by clicking on the
Pick Locator
button and hovering over any element in the browser window. While hovering over an element you will see the code needed to locate this element highlighted below. Clicking an element in the browser will add the locator into the field where you can then either tweak it or copy it into your code.

Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing
role, text and test id locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
. If Playwright finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient and uniquely identify the target element, so you don't have to worry about failing tests due to locators.

### Actionability logs​ {#actionability-logs}

By the time Playwright has paused on a
256| click action, it has already performed
actionability checks (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
that can be found in the log. This can help you understand what happened during your test and what Playwright did or tried to do. The log tells you if the element was visible, enabled and stable, if the locator resolved to an element, scrolled into view, and so much more. If actionability can't be reached, it will show the action as pending.

## Trace Viewer​ {#trace-viewer}

Playwright
Trace Viewer (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer)
is a GUI tool that lets you explore recorded Playwright traces of your tests. You can go back and forward through each action on the left side, and visually see what was happening during the action. In the middle of the screen, you can see a DOM snapshot for the action. On the right side you can see action details, such as time, parameters, return value and log. You can also explore console messages, network requests and the source code.

To learn more about how to record traces and use the Trace Viewer, check out the
Trace Viewer (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer)
guide.

By default, Playwright launches browsers in headless mode. See in our
Running tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/running-tests#run-tests-in-headed-mode)
guide how to run tests in headed mode.

On Linux agents, headed execution requires
Xvfb (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xvfb)
to be installed. Our
Docker image (https://playwright.dev/docs/docker)
and GitHub Action have Xvfb pre-installed. To run browsers in headed mode with Xvfb, add
`x

vfb-run`
before the actual command.

user_input: What's the simplest call to enter text into a form field, and does it also cover textareas and contenteditable?
reference: locator.fill() is the go-to: it focuses the field and fires an input event, and it handles <input>, <textarea> and [contenteditable] alike.
reference_contexts: Using locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill) is the easiest way to fill out the form fields. It focuses the element and triggers an input event with the entered text. It works for <input> , <textarea> and [contenteditable] elements.
llm_response:
The simplest and recommended call to enter text into a form field is `locator.fill()`. 

This method covers `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and `[contenteditable]` elements. It works by focusing the element and triggering an `input` event with the provided text.

user_input: What's the cleanest way to tick a checkbox or pick a radio button?
reference: Use setChecked() (or check()); it handles standard checkbox and radio inputs as well as elements that expose a checkbox role.
reference_contexts: Using locator.setChecked() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-checked) is the easiest way to check and uncheck a checkbox or a radio button. This method can be used with input[type=checkbox] , input[type=radio] and [role=checkbox] elements.
llm_response:
The cleanest and recommended way to tick a checkbox or pick a radio button is to use the `locator.setChecked()` method.

### Recommended Approach
`locator.setChecked()` is the preferred, locator-based method for setting the checked state of an element. It is the recommended alternative to discouraged methods like `page.setChecked` and `frame.setChecked`.

**Usage:**
```javascript
await page.getByRole('checkbox').setChecked(true);
```

### Alternative Approaches
Depending on your specific needs, you can also use the following locator-based methods:

*   **`locator.check()`**: Use this to ensure a checkbox or radio button is checked.
    *   *Usage:* `await page.getByRole('checkbox').check();`
*   **`locator.uncheck()`**: Use this to ensure a checkbox or radio button is unchecked.
    *   *Usage:* `await page.getByRole('checkbox').uncheck();`

### Discouraged Methods
The documentation explicitly discourages the use of the following methods in favor of the locator-based alternatives mentioned above:
*   `page.check` / `page.uncheck` / `page.setChecked`
*   `frame.check` / `frame.uncheck` / `frame.setChecked`
*   `elementHandle.check` / `elementHandle.uncheck` / `elementHandle.setChecked`

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright can interact with HTML Input elements such as text inputs, checkboxes, radio buttons, select options, mouse clicks, type characters, keys and shortcuts as well as upload files and focus elements.

## Text input​ {#text-input}

Using
locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill)
is the easiest way to fill out the form fields. It focuses the element and triggers an
`input`
event with the entered text. It works for
`<input>`
,
`<textarea>`
and
`[contenteditable]`
elements.


`// Text inputawaitpage.getByRole

('textbox').fill('Peter');// Date inputawaitpage.getByLabel('Birth date').fill('2020-02-02');// Time inputawaitpage.getByLabel('Appointment time').fill('13:15');// Local datetime inputawaitpage.getByLabel('Local time').fill('2020-03-02T05:15');`


## Checkboxes and radio buttons​ {#checkboxes-and-radio-buttons}

Using
locator.setChecked() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-checked)
is the easiest way to check and uncheck a checkbox or a radio button. This method can be used with
`input[type=checkbox]`
,
`input[type=radio]`
and
`[role=checkbox]`
elements.


`// Check the checkboxawaitpage.getByLabel('I agree to the terms above').check();// Assert the checked stateexpect(page.getByLabel('Subscribe to newsletter')).toBeChecked();// Select the radio buttonawaitpage.getByLabel('XL').check();`


## Select options​ {#select-options}

Selects one or multiple options in the
`<select>`
element with
locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option)
. You can specify option
`value`
, or
`label`
to select. Multiple options can be selected.


`// Single selection matching the value or labelawaitpage.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption('blue');// Single selection matching the label

awaitpage.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption({label:'Blue'});// Multiple selected itemsawaitpage.getByLabel('Choose multiple colors').selectOption(['red','green','blue']);`


## Mouse click​ {#mouse-click}

Performs a simple human click.


`// Generic clickawaitpage.getByRole('button').click();// Double clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').dblclick();// Right clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({button:'right'});// Shift + clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['Shift']});// Ctrl + click on Windows and Linux// Meta + click on macOSawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['ControlOrMeta']});// Hover over elementawaitpage.getByText('Item').hover();// Click the top left cornerawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({position:{x:0,y:0}});`


Under the hood, this and other pointer-related methods:

wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
wait for it to become displayed, i.e. not empty, no
`display:none`
, no
`visibility:hidden`
wait for it to stop moving, for example, until css transition finishes
scroll the element into view
wait for it to receive pointer events at the action point, for example, waits until element becomes non-obscured by other elements
retry if the element is detached during any of the above checks

#### Forcing the click​ {#forcing-the

-click}

Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the
actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
checks and force the click:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click({force:true});`


#### Programmatic click​ {#programmatic-click}

If you are not interested in testing your app under the real conditions and want to simulate the click by any means possible, you can trigger the
HTMLElement.click() (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/click)
behavior via simply dispatching a click event on the element with
locator.dispatchEvent() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-dispatch-event)
:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');`

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright can interact with HTML Input elements such as text inputs, checkboxes, radio buttons, select options, mouse clicks, type characters, keys and shortcuts as well as upload files and focus elements.

## Text input​ {#text-input}

Using
locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill)
is the easiest way to fill out the form fields. It focuses the element and triggers an
`input`
event with the entered text. It works for
`<input>`
,
`<textarea>`
and
`[contenteditable]`
elements.


`// Text inputawaitpage.getByRole
160|('textbox').fill('Peter');// Date inputawaitpage.getByLabel('Birth date').fill('2020-02-02');// Time inputawaitpage.getByLabel('Appointment time').fill('13:15');// Local datetime inputawaitpage.getByLabel('Local time').fill('2020-03-02T05:15');`


## Checkboxes and radio buttons​ {#checkboxes-and-radio-buttons}

Using
locator.setChecked() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-checked)
is the easiest way to check and uncheck a checkbox or a radio button. This method can be used with
`input[type=checkbox]`
,
`input[type=radio]`
and
`[role=checkbox]`
elements.


`// Check the checkboxawaitpage.getByLabel('I agree to the terms above').check();// Assert the checked stateexpect(page.getByLabel('Subscribe to newsletter')).toBeChecked();// Select the radio buttonawaitpage.getByLabel('XL').check();`


## Select options​ {#select-options}

Selects one or multiple options in the
`<select>`
element with
locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option)
. You can specify option
`value`
, or
`label`
to select. Multiple options can be selected.


`// Single selection matching the value or labelawaitpage.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption('blue');// Single selection matching the label
160|awaitpage.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption({label:'Blue'});// Multiple selected itemsawaitpage.getByLabel('Choose multiple colors').selectOption(['red','green','blue']);`


## Mouse click​ {#mouse-click}

Performs a simple human click.


`// Generic clickawaitpage.getByRole('button').click();// Double clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').dblclick();// Right clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({button:'right'});// Shift + clickawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['Shift']});// Ctrl + click on Windows and Linux// Meta + click on macOSawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({modifiers:['ControlOrMeta']});// Hover over elementawaitpage.getByText('Item').hover();// Click the top left cornerawaitpage.getByText('Item').click({position:{x:0,y:0}});`


Under the hood, this and other pointer-related methods:

wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
wait for it to become displayed, i.e. not empty, no
`display:none`
, no
`visibility:hidden`
wait for it to stop moving, for example, until css transition finishes
scroll the element into view
wait for it to receive pointer events at the action point, for example, waits until element becomes non-obscured by other elements
retry if the element is detached during any of the above checks

#### Forcing the click​ {#forcing-the
160|-click}

Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the
actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
checks and force the click:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click({force:true});`


#### Programmatic click​ {#programmatic-click}

If you are not interested in testing your app under the real conditions and want to simulate the click by any means possible, you can trigger the
HTMLElement.click() (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/click)
behavior via simply dispatching a click event on the element with
locator.dispatchEvent() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-dispatch-event)
:


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');`

user_input: How do I choose an option in a <select>, and can I pick several at once?
reference: Call selectOption() with the option's value or label; pass an array when you need multiple selected.
reference_contexts: Selects one or multiple options in the <select> element with locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option) . You can specify option value , or label to select. Multiple options can be selected.
llm_response:
To choose an option in a `<select>` element, the recommended approach is to use the `locator.selectOption()` method.

### How to choose an option
You can select options by providing a value, label, or index. The method supports the following:
*   **Value or Label:** Pass a string to match the option's value or label (e.g., `await locator.selectOption('blue');`).
*   **Object:** Pass an object to explicitly specify the label (e.g., `await locator.selectOption({ label: 'Blue' });`).
*   **Index:** Pass a number to match by index.

### Can I pick several at once?
Yes, you can select multiple options at once by passing an **array** of strings to the `locator.selectOption()` method. 

**Example for multiple selection:**
```javascript
await locator.selectOption(['red', 'green', 'blue']);
```

### Additional Information
*   **Behavior:** If the `<select>` element has the `multiple` attribute, all matching options are selected. If it does not have the `multiple` attribute, only the first option matching one of the passed values is selected.
*   **Alternatives:** While `page.selectOption`, `frame.selectOption`, and `elementHandle.selectOption` are available, locator-based selection (`locator.selectOption`) is the preferred approach.
*   **Verification:** You can verify that multiple values are selected using the `expect(locator).toHaveValues()` assertion.

user_input: If my page throws up an alert or confirm and I never handle it, will my test get stuck?
reference: No — with no dialog listener registered, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically, so they won't block the run.
reference_contexts: If there is no listener for page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) , all dialogs are automatically dismissed.
llm_response:
Yes, your test will get stuck. JavaScript dialogs (such as `alert`, `confirm`, `prompt`, or `beforeunload`) are modals that block further page execution until they are handled. If you register a `page.on('dialog')` listener, you must call either `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`; otherwise, the page will freeze and actions like `locator.click()` will never finish.

If you do not register any `page.on('dialog')` or `browserContext.on('dialog')` listeners, Playwright will automatically dismiss all dialogs for you.

user_input: Where should I keep saved login state, and how do I keep it out of version control?
reference: Stash it in a playwright/.auth directory and add that folder to .gitignore; tests then reuse the saved state to start already signed in.
reference_contexts: We recommend to create playwright/.auth directory and add it to your .gitignore . Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this playwright/.auth directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.
llm_response:
To keep saved login state, you should create a dedicated directory, such as `playwright/.auth`, to store your authentication state files (e.g., `user.json`, `admin.json`).

To keep this state out of version control, you must add the directory containing these files to your `.gitignore` file.

**Implementation examples:**

*   **Bash:**
    ```bash
    mkdir -p playwright/.auth
    echo -e "\nplaywright/.auth" >> .gitignore
    ```
*   **PowerShell:**
    ```powershell
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path playwright\.auth
    Add-Content -Path .gitignore "`r`nplaywright/.auth"
    ```
*   **Batch:**
    ```batch
    md playwright\.auth
    echo. >> .gitignore
    echo "playwright/.auth" >> .gitignore
    ```

The documentation strongly discourages checking these files into private or public repositories because they may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account.

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/auth>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4
llm_response:
To split your tests to run across several machines at once, you use the **sharding** feature.

### How to implement sharding
Pass the `--shard=x/y` command-line option to your test execution command, where `x` is the current shard index and `y` is the total number of shards. For example, to split your suite into four shards, you would run the following commands on four separate machines or CI jobs:

* `npx playwright test --shard=1/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=2/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=3/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=4/4`

### Balancing shards
The granularity of how tests are distributed depends on your configuration:

* **Recommended approach:** Use `fullyParallel: true` in your `playwright.config.ts` file. This enables test-level granularity, allowing Playwright to distribute individual tests across shards for a more balanced execution.
* **Alternative approach:** Without `fullyParallel: true`, Playwright defaults to file-level granularity. In this case, shards are assigned entire test files. To ensure balanced distribution, you must keep your test files small and evenly sized.

### Merging reports
Because each shard generates its own test report, you can merge them into a single report by using the `blob` reporter. Add the following to your `playwright.config.ts`:

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
});
```

The resulting blob reports can then be merged and converted into other Playwright report formats.

There are two different strategies when it comes to Test Isolation

arding with fullyParallel

When

is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This is the preferred mode for ensuring even load distribution when sharding, as Playwright can optimize shard execution based on the total number of tests.

Sharding without fullyParallel

Without the fullyParallel setting, Playwright Test defaults to file-level granularity, meaning entire test files are assigned to shards (note that the same file may be assigned to different shards across different projects). In this case, the number of tests per file can greatly influence shard distribution.

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,

are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure

user_input: Why do teams add data-testid attributes instead of leaning on text or role?
reference: Test ids survive copy and role changes, so those tests keep passing even when the UI wording shifts — the downside is they aren't user-facing.
reference_contexts: Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass. QA's and developers should define explicit test ids and query them with page.getByTestId() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-test-id) . However testing by test ids is not user facing.
llm_response:
Teams add `data-testid` attributes because testing by test IDs is the most resilient way of testing. Even if the text or role of an element changes, the test will still pass.

While user-facing locators like `role` and `text` are recommended for testing how a user perceives the page, teams use `data-testid` locators when:
* They choose to use the test ID methodology.
* They cannot locate an element by `role` or `text`.

To use this approach, developers and QA should define explicit test IDs and query them using `page.getByTestId()`. By default, Playwright uses the `data-testid` attribute, but you can configure a custom attribute name (such as `data-pw`) using the `testIdAttribute` option in your Playwright configuration file or by calling `selectors.setTestIdAttribute()`.

user_input: How do I watch the browser as my script runs and slow it down enough to follow along?
reference: Launch non-headless and pace each step with slowMo — e.g. chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 }).
reference_contexts:
// Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit
await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });
llm_response:
To watch the browser as your script runs and slow it down, you should use the following approaches:

### 1. Slow down operations
Use the `slowMo` option in the `launch` method to slow down Playwright operations by a specified number of milliseconds. This is useful for observing what is happening during execution.

```javascript
const browser = await chromium.launch({
  headless: false,
  slowMo: 50, // slows down by 50ms
});
```

### 2. Run in headed mode
By default, Playwright runs in headless mode. To see the browser window, you must set `headless: false` in your launch options:

```javascript
const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
```

### 3. Pause execution
To pause the script and inspect the browser, you can use `page.pause()` in your test code. This will open the Playwright Inspector, which allows you to step through each action of your test using the toolbar, see the current action highlighted in the test code, and view matching elements highlighted in the browser window.

```javascript
await page.pause();
```

If you want to configure the debugger to pause before the next action is executed, you can use `debugger.requestPause()`.

user_input: Is there a way to stop a test at a chosen line and poke around, instead of stepping through everything?
reference: Drop await page.pause() at that line and run in debug mode; the Inspector plays up to the pause and waits there when you hit Resume.
reference_contexts: Once you add a page.pause() call, run your tests in debug mode. Clicking the "Resume" button in the Inspector will run the test and only stop on the page.pause() .
llm_response:
Yes, you can stop a test at a chosen line to inspect it by using the `page.pause()` method.

When you add `await page.pause();` to your test code, the test will pause execution at that specific line when run in debug mode. This allows you to inspect variables and "poke around" without having to step through every preceding action.

To use this:
1. Add `await page.pause();` to your test at the desired location.
2. Run your tests in debug mode (e.g., by using the `--debug` flag or the "Debug Test" option in your IDE).
3. Once the test pauses, you can use the browser developer tools or the Playwright Inspector to interact with the page and inspect the state.

Alternatively, if you are using VS Code, you can set a breakpoint by clicking in the gutter next to a line number and then right-clicking the test to select **Debug Test**. The test will pause at that breakpoint, allowing you to inspect variables and step through the code.

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between 0 and workers - 1 . When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same parallelIndex and a new workerIndex .

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

## Worker index and parallel index​ {#worker-index-and-parallel-index}

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between
`0`
and
`workers - 1`

`parallelIndex`
and a new
`workerIndex`

`process.env.TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX`

and
testInfo.parallelIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-parallel-index)
.

user_input: Two problems with how our team writes tests. The recorder is the fastest way for people to get started, but the selectors it emits break on the next refactor, and half our app is behind a login so recording anything past the sign-in page means clicking through the form by hand every single time. Are both of these things the recorder can be told to handle?
reference: Both are, and they're separate mechanisms. On selectors: the generator isn't emitting raw CSS by accident — it inspects the page and picks what it judges the best locator, prioritising role, text and test id locators in that order, and when a candidate matches several elements it refines it until it uniquely identifies the target. So brittle output is usually a signal about the markup rather than the tool: give the elements you care about a test id (or accessible roles and names) and the recorder will prefer those. You can also use Pick Locator to grab and hand-tune a single locator rather than recording a whole flow. On the login: record the authentication once with `npx playwright codegen <url> --save-storage=auth.json`, which writes the cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB state at the end of the session, then start every later recording with `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>`, which restores that state so the app comes up already signed in and you record only the part you care about. That saved state is the same kind of artifact your suite consumes as storageState, so the recorded flow and the running tests can share it.
reference_contexts: Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing role, text and test id locators. If the generator finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient that uniquely identifies the target element.
The test generator can also generate a test while preserving authenticated state.

Run codegen with --save-storage to save cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data at the end of the session. This is useful to separately record an authentication step and reuse it later when recording more tests.

Run with --load-storage to consume the previously loaded storage from the auth.json. This way, all cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.
You can generate locators with the test generator.
llm_response:
Yes, the recorder can be used to address both of these issues.

### 1. Handling Fragile Selectors
The recorder (Codegen) is designed to generate reliable test code with proper locators. To manage selectors that break during refactors:
*   **Pick Locator Tool:** Instead of relying solely on the automatic recording, you can use the **Pick locator** tool from the testing sidebar. This allows you to hover over elements in the browser to see the generated locator, click to select the element, and then manually edit or fine-tune the locator in the field provided before copying it into your code.
*   **Manual Improvement:** After recording, you can inspect the generated `test-1.spec.ts` file and manually improve the locators if needed.

### 2. Handling Login
You do not need to click through the login form by hand every time. Playwright allows you to preserve the authenticated state:
*   **Save Storage State:** You can perform the authentication once and save the storage state (cookies, localStorage) to a file using the `--save-storage` option:
    `npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json`
*   **Load Authenticated State:** Once you have the `auth.json` file, you can reuse that authenticated state in future sessions or tests by running with the `--load-storage` option:
    `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json`
*   **Project Dependencies:** For your test suite, you can use **project dependencies** to define a setup test that runs once to authenticate, allowing you to reuse that state across multiple tests without logging in repeatedly.

<https://playwright.dev/docs/evaluating>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright scripts run in your Playwright environment. Your page scripts run in the browser page environment. Those environments don't intersect, they are running in different virtual machines in different processes and even potentially on different computers.

The
page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
API can run a JavaScript function in the context of the web page and bring results back to the Playwright environment. Browser globals like
`window`
and
`document`
can be used in
`evaluate`
.


`consthref=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>document.location.href);`


If the result is a Promise or if the function is asynchronous evaluate will automatically wait until it's resolved:


`conststatus=awaitpage.evaluate(async()=>{constresponse=awaitfetch(location.href);returnresponse.status;});`


## Different environments​ {#different-environments}

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing

environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

The following snippet is
WRONG
because it uses the variable directly:


`constdata='some data';constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>{// WRONG: there is no "data" in the web page.window.myApp.use(data);});`


The following snippet is
CORRECT
because it passes the value explicitly as an argument:


`constdata='some data';// Pass |data| as a parameter.constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(data=>{window.myApp.use(data);},data);`

page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
take a single optional argument. This argument can be a mix of
Serializable (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify#Description)
values and
JSHandle (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-jshandle)

<https://playwright.dev/docs/evaluating>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright scripts run in your Playwright environment. Your page scripts run in the browser page environment. Those environments don't intersect, they are running in different virtual machines in different processes and even potentially on different computers.

The
page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
API can run a JavaScript function in the context of the web page and bring results back to the Playwright environment. Browser globals like
`window`
and
`document`
can be used in
`evaluate`
.


`consthref=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>document.location.href);`


If the result is a Promise or if the function is asynchronous evaluate will automatically wait until it's resolved:


`conststatus=awaitpage.evaluate(async()=>{constresponse=awaitfetch(location.href);returnresponse.status;});`


## Different environments​ {#different-environments}

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing
281| environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

The following snippet is
WRONG
because it uses the variable directly:


`constdata='some data';constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>{// WRONG: there is no "data" in the web page.window.myApp.use(data);});`


The following snippet is

### Running Sequence​ {#running-sequence}

When working with tests that have a dependency, the dependency will always run first and once all tests from this project have passed, then the other projects will run in parallel.

Running order:

Tests in the 'setup' project run. Once all tests from this project have passed, then the tests from the dependent projects will start running.
Tests in the

'chromium', 'webkit' and 'firefox' projects run together. By default, these projects will
run in parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
, subject to the maximum workers limit.

If there are more than one dependency then these project dependencies will be run first and in parallel. If the tests from a dependency fails then the tests that rely on this project will not be run.

Running order:

Tests in the 'Browser Login' and 'DataBase' projects run in parallel:
'Browser Login' passes
❌ 'DataBase' fails!
