user_input: When I shard across CI jobs, how do workers, fullyParallel and retries interact to keep runs balanced and reliable?
reference: Inside each shard Playwright still runs worker processes; turning on fullyParallel shards at the individual-test level so each job gets an even slice rather than whole files. Keep retries enabled so that when a worker is torn down after a failure it simply restarts and re-runs the affected test.
reference_contexts: When fullyParallel: true is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs.
Workers are always shutdown after a test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures) to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.
If you enable retries , second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.
llm_response:
To keep runs balanced and reliable when sharding across CI jobs, these settings interact as follows:

### Balancing Shards
The granularity of how tests are balanced across shards is determined by the `fullyParallel` setting:
*   **`fullyParallel: true` (Recommended):** Tests are split at the individual test level. This is the preferred mode for ensuring an even load distribution, as Playwright optimizes shard execution based on the total number of tests.
*   **Without `fullyParallel`:** Tests are split at the file level. If test files are not evenly sized, some shards may run significantly more tests than others. In this case, you must manually organize your test files to be small and evenly sized to avoid imbalances.

### Reliability and Retries
*   **Worker Processes:** Workers are OS processes that run independently. Playwright reuses a single worker as much as possible to speed up testing, but workers are always shut down after a test failure to guarantee a pristine environment for subsequent tests.
*   **Retries:** When a test fails, it can be retried. If you are not using retries, all tests after a failure in a worker process are skipped. When using retries, all tests are retried together.
*   **Worker Indices:** Each worker is assigned a unique `workerIndex` and a `parallelIndex` (between `0` and `workers - 1`). When a worker is restarted (e.g., after a failure), the new process receives the same `parallelIndex` but a new `workerIndex`.
*   **CI Recommendation:** It is recommended to set `workers` to "1" in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility, as this ensures each test gets full system resources and avoids potential conflicts. If you have a powerful self-hosted CI system, you may enable parallel tests, but for wider parallelization, you should use sharding to distribute tests across multiple CI jobs.

### Interaction Summary
Sharding splits the test suite into smaller parts (using `--shard=x/y`), where each shard acts as an independent job. By combining `fullyParallel: true` with sharding, you achieve test-level granularity that balances the load across these independent CI jobs. Reliability is maintained by the worker lifecycle (shutting down after failures) and the ability to configure retries to handle flaky tests.

user_input: Should I use a globalSetup file or project dependencies for one-time setup, and why?
reference: Prefer project dependencies. Because a dependency is a real project that runs ahead of the others, it plugs into the runner properly — the setup shows up in the HTML report, is traced, and can use fixtures — whereas globalSetup misses some of that.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used.

Dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first.
llm_response:
You should use **project dependencies** for one-time setup. Playwright explicitly recommends this approach over the `globalSetup` configuration option because it provides full feature support and better integration with the test runner.

### Why use project dependencies?
Project dependencies are recommended because they offer several features that the `globalSetup` configuration option lacks:

*   **HTML Report Visibility:** Setup tests are shown as a separate project in the HTML report.
*   **Trace Recording:** Full traces are available for setup actions.
*   **Fixtures:** Playwright fixtures are fully supported within setup tests.
*   **Browser Management:** You can manage browsers via the `browser` fixture rather than manually via `browserType.launch()`.
*   **Configuration:** Options like `headless` or `testIdAttribute` are automatically applied to the setup project.
*   **Parallelism and Retries:** These are supported via standard configuration.

### Comparison Table

| Feature | Project Dependencies (Recommended) | `globalSetup` (Config Option) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **HTML report visibility** | ✅ Shown as a separate project | ❌ Not shown |
| **Trace recording** | ✅ Full trace available | ❌ Not supported |
| **Playwright fixtures** | ✅ Fully supported | ❌ Not supported |
| **Browser management** | ✅ Via `browser` fixture | ❌ Fully manual |
| **Parallelism and retries** | ✅ Supported | ❌ Not applicable |
| **Config options** | ✅ Automatically applied | ❌ Ignored |

### How to implement
To use project dependencies, define a specialized setup project in your `playwright.config.ts` and list it in the `dependencies` property of the projects that require it:

```javascript
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  projects: [
    { 
      name: 'setup', 
      testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/ 
    },
    { 
      name: 'chromium', 
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] }, 
      dependencies: ['setup'] 
    },
  ],
});
```

The setup code must be defined as a regular test using the `test()` function. You can also manage teardown by adding a `teardown` property to your setup project.

user_input: Our app registers a service worker for offline support. Every route handler I install works fine against a build with the worker disabled, but against the real build some requests reach the network untouched while others are intercepted, and which is which seems to change between runs. What decides whether a request is interceptable here, and what's the sane way to test against this app?
reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. That split is why interception looks inconsistent — you're catching some requests at one layer and missing others at the other, and which layer serves a given resource depends on the worker's cache state, hence the run-to-run variation. If you're doing ordinary network mocking, the documented answer is not to reason about this at all: set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the config's `use` options so the worker never registers and everything is page-owned and routable. Only if you specifically need to assert on the worker's own traffic should you leave them enabled and branch inside the handler on `route.request().serviceWorker()` — noting that calling .frame() on such a request throws, and that requests for updated worker scripts cannot currently be routed at all.
reference_contexts: If you're looking to do general network mocking, routing, and interception, please see the Network Guide first. Playwright provides built-in APIs for this use case that don't require the information below. However, if you're interested in requests made by Service Workers themselves, please read below.
To disable service workers, set testOptions.serviceWorkers to 'block'.

Only the Service Worker-owned request for the resource was routable via browserContext.route(); the Frame-owned events for data.json are not routeable, as they would not have even had the possibility to hit the external network since the Service Worker has a fetch handler registered.

await context.route('**', async route => { if (route.request().serviceWorker()) { // NB: calling route.request().frame() here would THROW await route.fulfill({ contentType: 'text/plain', status: 200, body: 'from sw', }); } else { await route.continue(); } });
Requests for updated Service Worker main script code currently cannot be routed.

user_input: Our GitHub Actions job installs cleanly — `npm ci` is green — and then every test fails at browser launch complaining about missing shared libraries. It's an ubuntu-latest runner, and the identical commit runs fine on all three of our developers' machines. What is the CI box missing that a laptop already has, and what's the durable way to fix it?
reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.
reference_contexts: Ensure CI agent can run browsers: Use our Docker image in Linux agents or install your dependencies using the CLI.
# Install NPM packages npm ci # Install Playwright browsers and dependencies npx playwright install --with-deps
The Command line tools can be used to install all operating system dependencies in CI.

GitHub Actions support running jobs in a container by using the jobs.<job_id>.container option. This is useful to not pollute the host environment with dependencies and to have a consistent environment for e.g. screenshots/visual regression testing across different operating systems.
llm_response:
The CI runner is missing the necessary operating system dependencies required to launch the browsers. While your local machine has these libraries installed, the `ubuntu-latest` runner in GitHub Actions does not include them by default.

The durable way to fix this is to use the `npx playwright install --with-deps` command in your GitHub Actions workflow. This command installs both the required browser binaries and the necessary system-level dependencies.

You should update the steps in your `.github/workflows/playwright.yml` file to include this command:

```yaml
- name: Install Playwright Browsers
  run: npx playwright install --with-deps
```

This approach is the recommended method for CI environments to ensure all required system dependencies are present.

## Properly handling Secrets​ {#properly-handling-secrets}

Artifacts like trace files, HTML reports or even the console logs contain information about your test execution. They can contain sensitive data like user credentials for a test user, access tokens to a staging backend, testing source code

, or sometimes even your application source code. Treat these files just as carefully as you treat that sensitive data. If you upload reports and traces as part of your CI workflow, make sure that you only upload them to trusted artifact stores, or that you encrypt the files before upload. The same is true for sharing artifacts with team members: Use a trusted file share or encrypt the files before sharing.

## Properly handling Secrets​ {#properly-handling-secrets}

Artifacts like trace files, HTML reports or even the console logs contain information about your test execution. They can contain sensitive data like user credentials for a test user, access tokens to a staging backend, testing source code
283|, or sometimes even your application source code. Treat these files just as carefully as you treat that sensitive data. If you upload reports and traces as part of your CI workflow, make sure that you only upload them to trusted artifact stores, or that you encrypt the files before upload. The same is true for sharing artifacts with team members: Use a trusted file share or encrypt the files before sharing.

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) s which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. They are fast and cheap to create and are completely isolated, even when running in a single browser. Playwright creates a context for each test, and provides a default Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page) in that context.

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.
llm_response:
Device emulation is applied per test through the configuration of browser contexts. Because Playwright creates isolated browser contexts for tests, emulation settings do not bleed into other tests.

### How emulation is applied
Emulation settings (viewport, user agent, touch, etc.) are applied using the following methods:

*   **Global Configuration:** You can define emulation settings in `playwright.config.ts` within the `use` object. These settings apply to all tests by default.
*   **Project Configuration:** You can use the `devices` utility from `@playwright/test` within the `projects` array in `playwright.config.ts` to assign specific browser profiles and emulation settings to different projects.
*   **Test-Level Configuration:** You can override or set emulation options for specific tests or `describe` blocks using `test.use()` within a test file.
*   **Explicit Context Creation:** When manually creating a context using `browser.newContext()`, you can pass emulation options directly to the method.

### Why it doesn't bleed into other tests
Emulation settings do not bleed between tests because Playwright provides **isolation** by creating separate browser contexts for each test. When you define emulation options via `test.use()` or project configurations, these settings are scoped to the browser context created for that specific test execution. Because each test runs in its own isolated context, changes to the viewport, user agent, or touch settings in one test do not affect the environment of any other test.

user_input: One fixture is slow, but I don't want to inflate every test's timeout. How do fixture and test timeouts relate, and what's the fix?
reference: A fixture's setup counts against the test's clock, so a sluggish one can trip test timeouts. Hand that fixture its own longer timeout through the tuple option and leave the test's timeout tight.
reference_contexts: By default, fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures) shares timeout with the test. However, for slow fixtures, especially worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures) ones, it is convenient to have a separate timeout. This way you can keep the overall test timeout small, and give the slow fixture more time.

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

user_input: Our CI machines are a lot slower than our laptops and I've been sprinkling per-assertion timeouts around to get the suite green, which is clearly the wrong shape. Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. The right fix for a uniformly slower machine is the config-level defaults, not per-assertion overrides.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout.
export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });
test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => { test.setTimeout(120_000); }); test.slow(); // Easy way to triple the default timeout
beforeAll and afterAll hooks have a separate timeout, by default equal to test timeout. You can change it separately for each hook by calling testInfo.setTimeout() inside the hook.

user_input: What's the reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element, and why avoid xpath=.. for it?
reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use xpath=.. . Note that this method is not as reliable, because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible.
llm_response:
The reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element is to use `locator.filter()`.

For example, if you have a child element located by `page.getByText('Hello')` and want to target its parent `<li>` element, you should use:

```javascript
const child = page.getByText('Hello');
const parent = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child });
```

You should avoid using `xpath=..` because it is not reliable; any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests.

### Locate by label​ {#locate-by-label}

Most form controls usually have dedicated labels that could be conveniently used to interact with the form. In this case, you can locate the control by its associated label using
page.getByLabel() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-label)
.

For example, consider the following DOM structure.

http://localhost:3000
Password

`<label>Password<inputtype="password"/></label>`


You can fill the input after locating it by the label text:


`awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('secret');`


When to use label locators
Use this locator when locating form fields.

### Locate by placeholder​ {#locate-by-placeholder}

Inputs may have a placeholder attribute to hint to the user what value should be entered. You can locate such an input using
page.getByPlaceholder() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-placeholder)
.

http://localhost:3000

`<inputtype="email"placeholder="name@example.com"/>`


You can fill the input after locating it by the placeholder text:

user_input: I'm adopting Page Object Models — how do I wire them so each test gets a ready-to-use page object without boilerplate?
reference: Wrap the POM in a fixture created with test.extend(): the fixture builds the page object (and can do setup/teardown around it), and any test just lists it as an argument. Fixtures are reusable across files, so every spec shares it.
reference_contexts: Page objects simplify authoring by creating a higher-level API which suits your application and simplify maintenance by capturing element selectors in one place and create reusable code to avoid repetition.
To create your own fixture, use test.extend() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-extend) to create a new test object that will include it.

Playwright Test uses
worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
to run test files. Similar to how test fixtures are set up for individual test runs, worker fixtures are set up for each worker process. That's where you can set up services, run servers, etc. Playwright Test will reuse the worker process for as many test files as it can, provided their worker fixtures match and hence environments are identical.

Below we'll create an
`account`
fixture that will be shared by all tests in the same worker, and override the
`page`
fixture to log in to this account for each test. To generate unique accounts, we'll use the
workerInfo.workerIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-workerinfo#worker-info-worker-index)
that is available to any test or fixture. Note the tuple-like syntax for the worker fixture - we have to pass
`{scope: 'worker'}`
so that test runner sets this fixture up once per worker.

In addition to only being run once per worker, worker-scoped fixtures also get a separate timeout equal to the default test timeout. You can change it by passing the
`timeout`
option. See
fixture timeout (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#fixture-timeout)
for more details.

my-test.ts

`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';typeAccount={username:string;password:string;};// Note that we pass worker

fixture types as a second template parameter.exportconsttest=base.extend<{},{account:Account}>({account:[async({browser},use,workerInfo)=>{// Unique username.constusername='user'+workerInfo.workerIndex;constpassword='verysecure';// Create the account with Playwright.constpage=awaitbrowser.newPage();awaitpage.goto('/signup');awaitpage.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);awaitpage.getByText('Sign up').click();// Make sure everything is ok.awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('result')).toHaveText('Success');// Do not forget to cleanup.awaitpage.close();// Use the account value.awaituse({username,password});},{scope:'worker'}],page:async({page,account},use)=>{// Sign in with our account.const{username,password}=account;awaitpage.goto('/signin');awaitpage.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);awaitpage.getByText('Sign in').click();awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('userinfo')).toHaveText(username);// Use signed-in page in the test.awaituse(page);},});export{expect}from'@playwright/test';`


## Automatic fixtures​ {#automatic-fixtures}

Automatic fixtures are set up for each test/worker, even when the test does not list them directly. To create an automatic fixture, use the tuple syntax and pass
`{ auto: true }`
.

Here is an example fixture that

automatically attaches debug logs when the test fails, so we can later review the logs in the reporter. Note how it uses the
TestInfo (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo)
object that is available in each test/fixture to retrieve metadata about the test being run.

my-test.ts

`importdebugfrom'debug';importfsfrom'fs';import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=base.extend<{saveLogs:void}>({saveLogs:[async({},use,testInfo)=>{// Collecting logs during the test.constlogs=[];debug.log=(...args)=>logs.push(args.map(String).join(''));debug.enable('myserver');awaituse();// After the test we can8');testInfo.attachments.push({name:'logs',contentType:'text/plain',path:logFile});}},{auto:true}],});export{expect}from'@playwright/test';`


## Fixture timeout​ {#fixture-timeout}

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.


`import{testasbase,expect}from'@playwright/test';consttest=base.extend<{slowFixture:string}>({slowFixture:[async({},use)=>{// ... perform a slow operation ...awaituse('

hello');},{timeout:60000}]});test('example test',async({slowFixture})=>{// ...});`


Unlike regular test-scoped fixtures, each
worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures)
fixture has its own timeout, equal to the test timeout. You can change the timeout for a worker-scoped fixture in the same way.

parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize)
.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Large test suites can be structured to optimize ease of authoring and maintenance. Page object models are one such approach to structure your test suite.

A page object represents a part of your web application. An e-commerce web application might have a home page, a listings page and a checkout page. Each of them can be represented by page object models.

Page objects
simplify authoring
by creating a higher-level API which suits your application and
simplify maintenance
by capturing element selectors in one place and create reusable code to avoid repetition.

user_input: Before a click, what does Playwright verify, and how does that relate to the waiting a plain click already does?
reference: A click runs actionability checks — attached, visible, stable, receives pointer events, enabled — and auto-waits for them. The pointer methods bake that same sequence in (down to scrolling into view), so you rarely need explicit waits.
reference_contexts: Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given timeout , action fails with the TimeoutError .
wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
llm_response:
Before performing a click, Playwright performs "actionability checks" to ensure the element is ready for the action. Specifically, for `locator.click()`, Playwright verifies that:

*   The locator resolves to exactly one element.
*   The element is visible.
*   The element is stable.
*   The element is enabled.
*   The element receives pointer events at the action point (e.g., it is not covered by an overlay).

This relates to the waiting a plain click already does because Playwright "auto-waits" for these checks to pass before executing the click. If these checks do not pass within the specified timeout, the action fails with a `TimeoutError`. This auto-waiting behavior is built-in, meaning you do not need to manually wait for the element to become available before clicking.

user_input: Where do downloaded files go, and why might they disappear before I can use them?
reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.
llm_response:
Downloaded files are stored in a temporary directory by default, which is cleaned up when the browser closes. Alternatively, you can specify a persistent directory for accepted downloads using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()`.

Downloaded files may disappear before you can use them because they are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed. Regardless of whether you use a temporary directory or a specified `downloadsPath`, the files are deleted upon the closure of the browser context in which they were created.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright can interact with the web page dialogs such as
alert (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
,
confirm (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/confirm)
,
prompt (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/prompt)
as well as
beforeunload (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/beforeunload_event)

Print (https://playwright.dev/docs/dialogs#print-dialogs)
.

## alert(), confirm(), prompt() dialogs​ {#alert-confirm-prompt-dialogs}

By default, dialogs are auto-dismissed by Playwright, so you don't have to handle them. However, you can register a dialog handler before the action that triggers the dialog to either
dialog.accept() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class
158|-dialog#dialog-accept)
or
dialog.dismiss() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-dialog#dialog-dismiss)
it.


`page.on('dialog',dialog=>dialog.accept());awaitpage.getByRole('button').click();`


note
page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog)
listener
must handle
the dialog. Otherwise your action will stall, be it
locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click)
or something else. That's because dialogs in Web are modals and therefore block further page execution until they are handled.

As a result, the following snippet will never resolve:

warning
WRONG!


`page.on('dialog',dialog=>console.log(dialog.message()));awaitpage.getByRole('button').click();// Will hang here`


note
If there is no listener for
page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog)
, all dialogs are automatically dismissed.

user_input: My manually-created context never produced a video file. How is video capture tied to the context lifecycle?
reference: Video is flushed when the browser context closes. With the test runner that happens automatically, but if you created the context yourself you must await context.close(), or the file won't be written.
reference_contexts: Videos are saved upon browser context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts) closure at the end of a test. If you create a browser context manually, make sure to await browserContext.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-close) .
When using Playwright as a Test Runner, browser contexts are created by default. Otherwise, you can create browser contexts manually.
llm_response:
Video capture is tied to the `BrowserContext` lifecycle. When you create a context manually, you must explicitly await `browserContext.close()` to ensure that recorded videos are properly saved to the disk.

If you do not await `browserContext.close()`, the video file will not be generated.

user_input: We rolled our own visual checks: capture a PNG, compare it byte-for-byte with a committed file, fail on any difference. It's unusable — it fails on the first run of any new test, it fails constantly on CI with what look like anti-aliasing differences, and there's no way to accept a legitimate design change short of regenerating files by hand. What does the built-in comparison do differently at each of those three points?
reference: Each of your three problems is a thing the built-in assertion already handles, because capturing an image and asserting on one are different operations. page.screenshot() just returns a buffer; expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() is a full comparison assertion. On first run there is no baseline, so instead of failing meaninglessly it takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match — which also settles animation and rendering noise — saves the result as the reference and reports that it wrote it; you commit that file. On CI, the baseline is keyed by environment: the snapshot name like example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png encodes the browser and platform (the project name replaces the browser when you use multiple projects) precisely because rendering, fonts and anti-aliasing differ across platforms, so Linux CI compares against its own baseline rather than your macOS one. And byte-exactness isn't required: `maxDiffPixels` (per assertion or globally under `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: ... }`) sets an allowance. When a change is intentional you re-baseline with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` rather than editing files.

chromium-darwin - the browser name and the platform. Screenshots differ between browsers and platforms due to different rendering, fonts and more, so you will need different snapshots for them. If you use multiple projects in your configuration file, project name will be used instead of chromium.
Sometimes you need to update the reference screenshot, for example when the page has changed. Do this with the --update-snapshots flag. npx playwright test --update-snapshots
export default defineConfig({ expect: { toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixels: 100 }, }, });
llm_response:
The built-in `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` method addresses your three issues as follows:

*   **Failing on the first run:** Instead of failing, the method automatically generates a reference "golden" file when one does not exist. It captures screenshots until two consecutive ones match to ensure stability before saving the baseline to the file system.
*   **Anti-aliasing/Flaky differences:** The method is designed to wait for "screenshot stabilization"—specifically, it continues capturing until two consecutive screenshots yield the same result—before performing the final comparison. Additionally, it supports configuration options like `threshold` (which defaults to `0.2` and uses the YIQ color space to calculate perceived color differences) and `maxDiffPixels` to allow for minor, acceptable variations.
*   **Accepting legitimate design changes:** You do not need to manually regenerate files. You can update the reference screenshots by running the test with the `--update-snapshots` command-line flag.

## Version 1.16​ {#version-116}

### 🎭 Playwright Test​ {#-playwright-test}

#### API Testing​ {#api-testing}

Playwright 1.16 introduces new
API Testing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
that lets you send requests to the server directly from Node.js! Now you can:

test your server API
prepare server side state before visiting the web application in a test
validate server side post-conditions after running some actions in the browser

To do a request on behalf of Playwright's Page, use
new
page.request (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-request)
API
:


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('context fetch',async({page})=>{// Do a GET request on behalf of pageconstresponse=awaitpage.request.get('http://example.com/foo.json');// ...});`


To do a stand-alone request from node.js to an API endpoint, use
new
request fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-fixtures#fixtures-request)
:


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('context fetch',async({request})=>{// Do a GET request on behalf of pageconstresponse=awaitrequest.get('http://example.com/foo.json');// ...});`


Read more about it in our

API testing guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/api-testing)
.

#### Response Interception​ {#response-interception}

It is now possible to do response interception by combining
API Testing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api-testing)
with
request interception (https://playwright.dev/docs/network#modify-requests)
.

For example, we can blur all the images on the page:


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';importjimpfrom'jimp';// image processing librarytest('response interception',async({page})=>{awaitpage.route('**/*.jpeg',asyncroute=>{constresponse=awaitpage._request.fetch(route.request());constimage=awaitjimp.read(awaitresponse.body());awaitimage.blur(5);awaitroute.fulfill({response,body:awaitimage.getBufferAsync('image/jpeg'),});});constresponse=awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev');expect(response.status()).toBe(200);});`


Read more about
response interception (https://playwright.dev/docs/network#modify-responses)
.

The HTML reporter has all the information about tests and their failures, including surfacing trace and image artifacts.

our reporters (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#html-reporter)
.

### 🎭 Playwright Test​ {#-playwright-test}

#### API Testing​ {#api-testing}

Playwright 1.16 introduces new
API Testing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
that lets you send requests to the server directly from Node.js! Now you can:

test your server API
prepare server side state before visiting the web application in a test
validate server side post-conditions after running some actions in the browser

To do a request on behalf of Playwright's Page, use
new
page.request (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-request)
API
:


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('context fetch',async({page})=>{// Do a GET request on behalf of pageconstresponse=awaitpage.request.get('http://example.com/foo.json');// ...});`


To do a stand-alone request from node.js to an API endpoint, use
new
request fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-fixtures#fixtures-request)
:


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('context fetch',async({request})=>{// Do a GET request on behalf of pageconstresponse=awaitrequest.get('http://example.com/foo.json');// ...});`


Read more about it in our

API testing guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/api-testing)
.

#### Response Interception​ {#response-interception}

It is now possible to do response interception by combining
API Testing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api-testing)
with
request interception (https://playwright.dev/docs/network#modify-requests)
.

For example, we can blur all the images on the page:


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';importjimpfrom'jimp';// image processing librarytest('response interception',async({page})=>{awaitpage.route('**/*.jpeg',asyncroute=>{constresponse=awaitpage._request.fetch(route.request());constimage=awaitjimp.read(awaitresponse.body());awaitimage.blur(5);awaitroute.fulfill({response,body:awaitimage.getBufferAsync('image/jpeg'),});});constresponse=awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev');expect(response.status()).toBe(200);});`


Read more about
response interception (https://playwright.dev/docs/network#modify-responses)
.

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/auth>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

run in parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
, subject to the maximum workers limit.

If there are more than one dependency then these project dependencies will be run first and in parallel. If the tests from a dependency fails then the tests that rely on this project will not be run.

reference: The scan and the regression are aimed at different things, which is why one sailed past the other. An automated scan — the documented approach uses the @axe-core/playwright package, where you await `new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze()` and assert the returned `violations` array is empty — detects *rule* violations such as missing or invalid properties. It has no opinion about whether the structure is the one you intended, and the docs are explicit that many accessibility problems can only be found through manual testing, recommending a combination of automated scans, manual assessment and inclusive user testing. What your refactor changed was the shape of the accessibility tree, and that is what an aria snapshot pins: expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot() captures a YAML representation of the accessibility tree — the hierarchy of accessible elements with their roles, attributes, values and text, with indentation carrying the nesting — and fails when the current tree stops matching it. Order and nesting are part of that representation, so a moved section shows as a diff. The two compose: accessibility tests are ordinary tests, so you can put both in one spec or keep separate ones. Bear in mind the tradeoff the docs draw between the styles — targeted assertions check one specific condition and get verbose over complex structures, while snapshots capture whole-structure state and are best for outputs that rarely change shape, which also means they need deliberate re-baselining when a change is intentional.

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles, attributes, values, and text content. The structure follows a tree-like syntax, where each node represents an accessible element, and indentation indicates nested elements.

The automated accessibility scan using the `axe-core` engine is designed to detect common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties, poor color contrast, and interactive elements with duplicate IDs.

The regression you experienced—where the sections of your settings panel were read in the wrong order—is a structural issue that would have been caught by **ARIA Snapshots**. ARIA snapshots provide a YAML representation of the page's accessibility tree, and the `toMatchAriaSnapshot` assertion verifies that the current accessibility tree matches the expected structure. Because this comparison is order-sensitive, it ensures that the elements appear in the accessibility tree in the expected sequence.

Yes, both can live in the same test. You can integrate both the `AxeBuilder.analyze()` scan and the `toMatchAriaSnapshot` assertion into your existing test cases to verify both the presence of valid properties and the correct structural order of your UI components.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright can be used to test your application for many types of accessibility issues.

A few examples of problems this can catch include:

Text that would be hard to read for users with vision impairments due to poor color contrast with the background behind it
UI controls and form elements without labels that a screen reader could identify
Interactive elements with duplicate IDs which can confuse assistive technologies

The following examples rely on the
@axe-core/playwright (https://npmjs.org/@axe-core/playwright)
package which adds support for running the
axe accessibility testing engine (https://www.deque.com/axe/)
as part of your Playwright tests.

Disclaimer
Automated accessibility tests can detect some common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties. But many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. We recommend using a combination of automated testing, manual accessibility assessments, and inclusive user testing.
For manual assessments, we recommend
Accessibility Insights for Web (https://accessibilityinsights.io/docs/web/overview/?referrer=playwright-accessibility-testing-js)
, a free and open source dev tool that walks you through assessing a website for
WCAG 2.1 AA (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/?currentsidebar=%23col_customize&levels=aaa)
coverage.

A common question when adding accessibility tests to an application is "how do I suppress known violations?" The following examples demonstrate a few techniques you can use.

### Excluding individual elements from a scan​ {#excluding-individual-elements-from-a-scan}

If your application contains a few specific elements with known issues, you can use
AxeBuilder.exclude() (https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core-npm/blob/develop/packages/playwright/README.md#axebuilderexcludeselector-string--string)
to exclude them from being scanned until you're able to fix the issues.

This is usually the simplest option, but it has

some important downsides:

`exclude()`
will exclude the specified elements
and all of their descendants

`exclude()`
will prevent
all
rules from running against the specified elements, not just the rules corresponding to known issues.

If the element in question is used repeatedly in many pages, consider
using a test fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/accessibility-testing#using-a-test-fixture-for-common-axe-configuration)
to reuse the same
`AxeBuilder`
configuration across multiple tests.

### Disabling individual scan rules​ {#disabling-individual-scan-rules}

If your application contains many different preexisting violations of a specific rule, you can use
AxeBuilder.disableRules() (https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core-npm/blob/develop/packages/playwright/README.md#axebuilderdisablerulesrules-stringarray)
to temporarily disable individual rules until you're able to fix the issues.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright can be used to test your application for many types of accessibility issues.

A few examples of problems this can catch include:

Text that would be hard to read for users with vision impairments due to poor color contrast with the background behind it

Interactive elements with duplicate IDs which can confuse assistive technologies

@axe-core/playwright (https://npmjs.org/@axe-core/playwright)

axe accessibility testing engine (https://www.deque.com/axe/)

Accessibility Insights for Web (https://accessibilityinsights.io/docs/web/overview/?referrer=playwright-accessibility-testing-js)
, a free and open source dev tool that walks you through assessing a website for

coverage.

user_input: I need to assert that every row in our pricing table renders right-aligned, which isn't in the DOM anywhere — it's a computed style. Nothing on the locator exposes it, and my first attempt at reaching into the page came back with undefined for the threshold I was comparing against, even though it's a plain number defined right above the call.
reference: Two boundaries are in play. First, to get at computed style you have to run code in the page: a locator resolves to elements but only exposes what the API models, so anything the API doesn't cover you obtain with evaluate. For the whole set at once use locator.evaluateAll(), whose callback receives the array of matching elements — e.g. `await page.locator('td.price').evaluateAll(els => els.map(e => getComputedStyle(e).textAlign))` — returning an ordinary array back into the test. Second, that callback executes in the browser, in a different context from your test file, so it cannot close over test variables; that's why your threshold was undefined rather than throwing at definition. Pass it explicitly as the second argument: `locator.evaluateAll((els, limit) => ..., limit)`. Whatever you return has to be serializable to cross back — return the strings or numbers you want to assert on, not DOM nodes.
reference_contexts: The code inside locator.evaluateAll() runs in the page, you can call any DOM apis there.
const rows = page.getByRole('listitem'); const texts = await rows.evaluateAll( list => list.map(element => element.textContent));

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.
llm_response:
To assert that every row in your pricing table renders right-aligned, you should use the `expect(locator).toHaveCSS()` assertion. This is an async assertion that automatically retries until the specified computed CSS property is detected.

For your specific case, you would use it as follows:

```javascript
await expect(locator).toHaveCSS('text-align', 'right');
```

**Key details regarding this approach:**
*   **Computed Styles:** `toHaveCSS` is designed specifically to verify computed CSS styles of an element.
*   **Automatic Retries:** It functions as an async assertion that automatically retries the check until the property is detected.
*   **Handling Multiple Rows:** If you have a locator representing multiple rows (e.g., `page.locator('.pricing-row')`), you can iterate through them or use `nth()` to target specific rows. If you need to verify all of them, you can use `locator.evaluateAll()` to check the computed style of each element within the page context if you prefer a single batch operation, but `toHaveCSS` is the recommended built-in assertion for verifying CSS properties on a locator.
*   **Regarding your "undefined" issue:** Ensure you are passing the CSS property name and the expected value as strings to `toHaveCSS`. If you were previously attempting to compare a value manually (e.g., by reaching into the page and getting `undefined`), using the built-in `toHaveCSS` assertion avoids this by handling the retrieval and comparison of the computed style for you.

reference: Define a project per device and spread a device descriptor into its use (e.g. devices['Pixel 5']). Projects let you run the same tests under different configurations, and each project applies its device's emulated parameters.
reference_contexts: By using projects you can run your tests in multiple browsers such as chromium, webkit and firefox as well as branded browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. Playwright can also run on emulated tablet and mobile devices.

Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

With Playwright you can test your app on any browser as well as emulate a real device such as a mobile phone or tablet. Simply configure the devices you would like to emulate and Playwright will simulate the browser behavior such as
`"userAgent"`

shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

reference: Declare an 'option' fixture with a default value, then override that value per project in the config's use block. The fixture reads the option, so each project drives its own behavior in a type-safe way.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
You can also use projects to run the same tests in different configurations. For example, you can run the same tests in a logged-in and logged-out state.

These agents can be used independently, sequentially, or as the chained calls in the agentic loop. Using them sequentially will produce test coverage for your product.

executes the test suite and automatically repairs failing tests

user_input: How do I tag tests to run just those from the CLI, and also carve tests into subsets at the project level?
reference: Label tests with @-tokens and select them at runtime via --grep. For a more structural cut, group tests into separate projects and let each project's own filter — say a testMatch on the file name — decide what it runs.
reference_contexts: You can now run tests that have a particular tag with --grep (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli#all-options) command line option.

We can split tests into projects and use filters to run a subset of tests. For example, we can create a project that runs tests using a filter matching all tests with a specific file name. We can then have another group of tests that ignore specific test files.
llm_response:
To tag tests and run only those from the CLI, or to carve tests into subsets at the project level, use the following approaches:

### Tagging and Running Tests from the CLI
1.  **Tagging:** You can tag a test by adding a `tag` property to the test details object or by including a tag starting with `@` in the test title.
    *   **Example:** `test('test login page', { tag: '@fast' }, async ({ page }) => { ... });`
2.  **CLI Filtering:** Use the `--grep` command-line option to run only tests with a specific tag.
    *   **Example:** `npx playwright test --grep @fast`
    *   You can also use `--grep-invert` to skip tests with a certain tag.

### Carving Tests into Subsets at the Project Level
To carve tests into subsets at the project level, use the `testProject.grep` configuration option within your `playwright.config.ts` file. This allows you to filter the execution of tests for specific projects using regular expressions.

*   **Configuration:**
    ```typescript
    // playwright.config.ts
    import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
    export default defineConfig({
      projects: [
        {
          name: 'subset-project',
          grep: /@smoke/, // Only runs tests with the @smoke tag
        },
      ],
    });
    ```
*   **Behavior:** The `grep` option filters tests based on a regular expression tested against a string consisting of the project name, test file name, `test.describe` name, test name, and test tags.

### Additional Options
*   **Project Selection:** You can run specific subsets of tests defined as projects using the `--project` CLI flag.
    *   **Example:** `npx playwright test --project=chromium`
*   **Sharding:** To distribute tests across multiple machines (carving the suite into subsets), use the `--shard` command-line option.
    *   **Example:** `npx playwright test --shard=1/3`

user_input: I want to parameterize the same tests with different values — both at the test level and across environments. How do these two levels differ?
reference: You can parameterize at the test level or the project level. Project-level parameterization uses option fixtures whose values you set in each project's config, which is how you run the same tests against different environments.
reference_contexts: You can either parameterize tests on a test level or on a project level.

Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
llm_response:
You can parameterize tests at the test level or the project level. These two levels differ in their scope and implementation:

*   **Test Level:** You can parameterize tests by iterating over a data set (e.g., using `.forEach()`) within a test file. This allows you to run the same test logic with different values (such as names or expected results) for each iteration.
*   **Project Level:** You can parameterize tests by defining multiple test projects in your `playwright.config.ts` file. This approach allows you to run the same tests with different configurations, such as different environments (e.g., staging vs. production) or different options (e.g., passing a `person` value to different projects). Projects are used to group tests that share the same configuration.

Additionally, you can differentiate between environments by using the `testConfig.tag` property to tag tests with an environment name, which is useful for merging reports from multiple environments. Environment variables (e.g., via `.env` files or command-line arguments) can also be used to configure tests for different environments.

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes

are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:


`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locallyworkers:process.env.CI?2:undefined,});`


## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`


## Parallelize tests in a single file​ {#parallelize-tests-in-a

-single-file}

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'parallel'});test('runs in parallel 1',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('runs in parallel 2',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


Alternatively, you can opt-in all tests into this fully-parallel mode in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// runs all tests in all files of a specific project in parallelprojects:[{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome']},fullyParallel:true,},]});`


## Serial mode​ {#serial-mode}

You can annotate inter-dependent tests

as serial. If one of the serial tests fails, all subsequent tests are skipped. All tests in a group are retried together.

note
Using serial is not recommended. It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be run independently.


`import{test,typePage}from'@playwright/test';// Annotate entire file as serial.test.describe.configure({mode:'serial'});letpage:Page;test.beforeAll(async({browser})=>{page=awaitbrowser.newPage();});test.afterAll(async()=>{awaitpage.close();});test('runs first',async()=>{awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev/');});test('runs second',async()=>{awaitpage.getByText('Get Started').click();});`

<https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Tests written with Playwright execute in isolated clean-slate environments called browser contexts. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures.

## What is Test Isolation?​ {#what-is-test-isolation}

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using
BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext)
s which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. They are fast and cheap to create and

shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes
0| are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:


`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locallyworkers:process.env.CI?2:undefined,});`


## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`

user_input:
My click fails on a page that has both a hidden and a visible button. Code:

await page.locator('button').click();

Error:

Error: strict mode violation: locator('button') resolved to 2 elements

How do I click only the visible one?
reference: The locator matched both buttons and threw a strictness violation. Filter to only visible elements, e.g. await page.locator('button').filter({ visible: true }).click(); (or use the css :visible pseudo-class). Locators are strict and throw when more than one element matches.
reference_contexts: Consider a page with two buttons, the first invisible and the second visible (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#visible) .
This will find both buttons and throw a strictness (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#strictness) violation error:
This will only find a second button, because it is visible, and then click it.
await page.locator('button').filter({ visible: true }).click();
llm_response:
To click only the visible button when multiple elements match your locator, you should use the `.filter()` method to narrow the selection to the visible element:

```javascript
await page.locator('button').filter({ visible: true }).click();
```

Alternatively, you can use the `:visible` pseudo-class within a CSS selector:

```javascript
await page.locator('button:visible').click();
```

page.on('dialog', dialog => console.log(dialog.message()));

reference: The dialog listener must actually handle the dialog by calling dialog.accept() or dialog.dismiss(); otherwise the action stalls because dialogs are modals that block page execution. Fix by accepting/dismissing, e.g. page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept()).

That's because dialogs in Web are modals and therefore block further page execution until they are handled.

llm_response:
The reason your test hangs is that JavaScript dialogs (such as `confirm`) are modal and block further page execution until they are handled. While you have a listener that logs the message, your listener does not explicitly tell the dialog to proceed or close, which causes the page to freeze and the `click()` action to never resolve.

To fix this, your `page.on('dialog', ...)` listener must call either `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`.

**Recommended approach:**
Register a dialog handler before the action that triggers the dialog to explicitly handle it:

```javascript
page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept()); // or dialog.dismiss()
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete card' }).click();
```

**Key points from the documentation:**
*   **Mandatory handling:** If a `page.on('dialog')` listener is present, it **must** handle the dialog. If it does not, the action (such as `locator.click()`) will stall and never finish.
*   **Default behavior:** If no `page.on('dialog')` listener is present, Playwright automatically dismisses all dialogs. By adding your own listener, you overrode this default behavior, which is why you must now manually call `accept()` or `dismiss()` to allow the test to continue.

This assertion fails on our CI runner maybe one run in four, and never locally. The message says it received an empty string, but if I put a screenshot immediately before the assertion the button clearly has its label in the image.

await expect(page.locator('button')).toHaveText('my text');

Error: expect(received).toHaveText(expected)
Expected string: "my text"
Received string: ""
Call log:
  - expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms
  - waiting for "locator('button')"

The test as a whole is nowhere near its own limit — it finishes in about eight seconds when it passes. So what ran out, and is bumping it the right response or am I papering over something?
reference: This is the auto-retrying assertion timing out after its default 5-second expect timeout because the element's text stayed empty. The expect timeout is separate from the test timeout; you can raise it per-assertion (e.g. { timeout: 10_000 }) or via testConfig.expect, but first confirm the element actually receives the expected text.
reference_contexts: Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout. It produces the following error:

example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================

Error: expect(received).toHaveText(expected)

Expected string: "my text"
Received string: ""
Call log:
  - expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms
  - waiting for "locator('button')"
await expect(locator).toHaveText('hello', { timeout: 10_000 });
llm_response:
The assertion is failing because it has reached its **assertion timeout**, which defaults to 5 seconds. This timeout is separate from the overall test timeout.

The error message indicates that while the assertion was polling the locator, it received an empty string (`""`) instead of the expected text (`"my text"`) within that 5-second window.

### Is bumping the timeout the right response?
Bumping the timeout is not necessarily the right response; it may be "papering over" a race condition where the element is present in the DOM but its text content has not yet been populated or updated by the application.

### Recommended approach
To address flakiness, the documentation recommends the following:

1.  **Use `useInnerText`**: If you are asserting text, you can use the `useInnerText` option with `expect(locator).toHaveText()` to potentially improve stability.
    ```javascript
    await expect(locator).toHaveText('my text', { useInnerText: true });
    ```
2.  **Verify the Locator**: Ensure your locator is specific enough. If the locator matches multiple elements or an element that is not yet fully rendered, the assertion may fail.
3.  **Configure Assertion Timeout**: If the application is genuinely slow and requires more time to populate the text, you can increase the timeout for the assertion. You can do this for a single assertion by configuring a custom `expect` instance:
    ```javascript
    const slowExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 10000 });
    await slowExpect(page.locator('button')).toHaveText('my text');
    ```
    Alternatively, you can set the default timeout for all web-first assertions globally via the `testConfig.expect` value in your test configuration.

If the issue persists, consider using `expect.poll` or `expect.toPass` for more complex scenarios where you need to retry blocks of code until a condition is met.

## Assertions​ {#assertions}

Playwright includes
test assertions (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions)
in the form of
`expect`
function. To make an assertion, call
`expect(value)`
and choose a matcher that reflects the expectation.

Playwright includes async matchers that wait until the expected condition is met. Using these matchers makes tests non-flaky and resilient. For example, this code waits until the page gets the title containing "Playwright":

Our nightly regression job has one spec that imports a 30MB fixture and walks a long onboarding wizard. It genuinely takes about a minute and it is genuinely doing useful work — nothing is stuck. It fails every night with:

example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================
Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.

I don't want to raise the limit for the other 400 tests, because a test that hangs should still fail fast. How do I give room to this one only?
reference: This is the per-test timeout (30s default) being exceeded. Increase it for a single test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or use test.slow() to triple the default. Globally you can set timeout in the config.

Playwright comes with three Playwright Test Agents out of the box:
🎭 planner
,
🎭 generator
and
🎭 healer
.

These agents can be used independently, sequentially, or as the chained calls in the agentic loop. Using them sequentially will produce test coverage for your product.

🎭 planner
explores the app and produces a Markdown test plan
🎭 generator
transforms the Markdown plan into the Playwright Test files
🎭 healer
executes the test suite and automatically repairs failing tests

# Agents | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-agents>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright comes with three Playwright Test Agents out of the box:
🎭 planner
,
🎭 generator
and
🎭 healer
.

These agents can be used independently, sequentially, or as the chained calls in the agentic loop. Using them sequentially will produce test coverage for your product.

🎭 planner
explores the app and produces a Markdown test plan
🎭 generator
transforms the Markdown plan into the Playwright Test files
🎭 healer
executes the test suite and automatically repairs failing tests

### Getting Started​ {#getting-started}

Start with adding Playwright Test Agent definitions to your project using the
`init-agents`
command. These definitions should be regenerated whenever Playwright is updated to pick up new tools and instructions.

VS Code
Claude Code
OpenCode

`npx playwright init-agents--loop=vscode`


`npx playwright init-agents--loop=claude`


`npx playwright init-agents--loop=opencode`


note
VS Code v1.
170|105 (released October 9, 2025) is needed for the agentic experience to function properly in VS Code.

Once the agents have been generated, you can use your AI tool of choice to command these agents to build Playwright Tests.
