user_input:
My filter-by-descendant assertion doesn't find the right card. Code:

await expect(page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('list').getByText('Product 2') }))
    .toHaveCount(1);

It matches 0. Why?
reference: The filtering locator is queried starting from the original listitem match, not the document root. getByRole('list') starts from the <ul>, which is outside the matched <li>, so nothing matches. Make the inner locator relative, e.g. filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Product 2' }) }).
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root. Therefore, the following will not work, because the filtering locator starts matching from the <ul> list element that is outside of the <li> list item matched by the original locator:

await page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Product 2' }) })
    .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
    .click();
llm_response:
The assertion fails because the filtering locator is relative to the original locator, not the document root. 

In your code, `page.getByRole('list').getByText('Product 2')` attempts to find a `<ul>` (list) element inside the `<li>` (listitem) element. Because the list element is outside the list item, the filter does not find a match.

To fix this, ensure the filtering locator matches an element that is a descendant of the original locator. According to the documentation, the filtering locator must be relative to the original locator. For example, if you are looking for a heading inside a list item, you should use:

```javascript
await expect(page
    .getByRole('listitem')
    .filter({ has: page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Product 2' }) }))
    .toHaveCount(1);
```

The documentation explicitly notes that using `page.getByRole('list')` inside the filter will not work because it starts matching from the list element, which is outside the `<li>` being filtered.

### Interactions​ {#interactions}

Performing actions starts with locating elements. Playwright uses
Locators API (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
for that. Locators represent a way to find element(s) on the page at any moment. Learn more about the
different types (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
of locators available.

Playwright waits for the element to be
actionable (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
before performing the action, so you don't need to wait for it to become available.


`//

user_input:
A colleague added visual coverage to the checkout page and CI went red on the very first run of the new test — before anyone had changed any styling. The message doesn't read like a normal assertion failure and there's no diff image in the report, just this:

await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot();

Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

Re-running the job locally doesn't produce the error. Is the test wrong, or is CI wrong?
reference: No. On first execution there is no golden file yet, so Playwright takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match, saves the last as the reference, and reports this message. The generated snapshot is ready to be committed; subsequent runs compare against it.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test includes the ability to produce and visually compare screenshots using await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() . On first execution, Playwright test will generate reference screenshots. Subsequent runs will compare against the reference.
Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

That's because there was no golden file yet. This method took a bunch of screenshots until two consecutive screenshots matched, and saved the last screenshot to file system. It is now ready to be added to the repository.
llm_response:
Neither the test nor CI is "wrong." The error message you are seeing is expected behavior when running `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` for the first time.

According to the documentation, when you run this assertion for the first time, there is no "golden file" (baseline image) yet. Playwright captures the current page state, saves it to the file system, and throws that error to inform you that it has written the "actual" screenshot. This file is now ready to be added to your repository as the baseline for future runs.

The reason you do not see this error when re-running the job locally is likely because the baseline image was already generated and saved to your local file system during the first run.

To resolve this:
1. Locate the generated snapshot file (e.g., `example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png`).
2. Commit this file to your version control system.
3. Subsequent runs in CI will compare the current page state against this committed baseline rather than failing.

Note that screenshot rendering can vary based on the host OS, browser version, and hardware. For consistent results, ensure that the environment where the baseline is generated matches the environment where your CI tests run.

reference: :has-text() matches any element containing the text, so used alone it matches many elements including <body>. Combine it with another CSS specifier, e.g. await page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")').click();
reference_contexts: Note that :has-text() should be used together with other CSS specifiers, otherwise it will match all the elements containing specified text, including the <body> .
llm_response:
The `:has-text("Playwright")` selector matches any element containing that text, including the `<body>` tag and other parent containers, because it searches for the substring anywhere within the element's descendants.

To narrow this to the specific element you want, you should avoid using `:has-text()` alone. Instead, use it in combination with other selectors or use more specific locator methods.

### Recommended Approaches

1.  **Combine with other selectors:** Use `:has-text()` alongside a more specific element type to avoid matching the `<body>`.
    *   *Example:* `page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")').click();`
2.  **Use `locator.filter()`:** This is the preferred way to narrow down an existing locator by text content.
    *   *Example:* `await page.getByRole('button').filter({ hasText: 'Playwright' }).click();`
3.  **Use specific locator methods:** Whenever possible, prioritize user-visible locators like `getByRole`, `getByText`, or `getByTestId` to uniquely identify the element.
    *   *Example:* `await page.getByText('Playwright', { exact: true }).click();`

If you have multiple matches and need to select a specific one, you can use:
*   **`locator.first()`**: To select the first match.
*   **`locator.nth(index)`**: To select a specific match by its zero-based index.

llm_response:
To wait for readiness in your single-page app, you should avoid `waitForLoadState('networkidle')`, as the documentation explicitly discourages its use for testing. Instead, you should rely on web assertions to assess readiness.

The recommended approach is to use **locator-based assertions** or **`locator.waitFor()`**:

*   **Web Assertions:** Use assertions like `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()` to verify that the specific elements you expect to be present are ready. Playwright automatically waits for elements to satisfy the required state (such as visibility) before proceeding.
*   **`locator.waitFor()`:** If you need to explicitly wait for an element to reach a specific state (e.g., visible or attached) before performing further actions, use `locator.waitFor()`. This is the modern, recommended alternative to older methods like `page.waitForSelector`.

**Example:**
Instead of waiting for the network to be idle, wait for the specific content that indicates the page is ready:

```javascript
await page.goto('/dashboard');
// Playwright will auto-wait for the heading to be visible
await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Welcome' })).toBeVisible();
```

If you have specific background processes or analytics that cause the network to never reach an "idle" state, these assertion-based approaches will allow your test to proceed as soon as the UI is ready, rather than waiting for the network to stop activity.

reference_contexts: It might be that you are using a mock tool such as Mock Service Worker (MSW). While this tool works out of the box for mocking responses, it adds its own Service Worker that takes over the network requests, hence making them invisible to browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) .

If you're using Playwright's native browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) , and it appears network events are missing, disable Service Workers by setting serviceWorkers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context-option-service-workers) to 'block' .
llm_response:
The reason your Playwright route is not firing is likely because you are using Mock Service Worker (MSW). MSW installs its own Service Worker that intercepts network requests before they reach Playwright's `page.route()` or `browserContext.route()` handlers, making those requests invisible to Playwright.

To resolve this, you have two options:

1.  **Disable Service Workers:** If you want to use Playwright's native routing, you must disable Service Workers by setting `serviceWorkers` to `'block'` in your browser context configuration.
2.  **Use MSW Handlers:** If you prefer to continue using MSW, you should use the `router` fixture (available in component testing) to register your MSW handlers instead of using `page.route()`. You can do this by calling `router.use(handlers)` with your existing MSW request handlers.

reference_contexts: Targeted input actions in Playwright automatically distinguish between labels and controls, so you can target the label to perform an action on the associated control.

However, other methods will target the label itself, for example expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) will assert the text content of the label, not the input field.

llm_response:
The reason your assertion fails to read the value you typed is that `expect(locator).toHaveText()` is designed to verify the text content of the element matched by the locator, not the value of an input field. When you target a `label` element, `toHaveText` asserts against the label's caption text.

While Playwright's targeted input actions (like `.fill()`) automatically distinguish between labels and controls to perform actions on the associated input, assertion methods do not perform this same retargeting.

To verify the value entered into an input field, you must use the following:

*   **Recommended approach:** Use `expect(locator).toHaveValue()`. This assertion is specifically designed to verify that an input element contains a designated value.
*   **Alternative:** If you need to retrieve the value for other purposes, use `locator.inputValue()`, which returns the value for `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `<select>` elements.

To fix your test, update your assertion to target the input field directly (e.g., by using `page.getByLabel('Password')`) and use `toHaveValue`:

```javascript
await expect(page.getByLabel('Password')).toHaveValue('your-expected-value');
```

Playwright uses simplified glob patterns for URL matching in network interception methods like

A single
`*`
matches any characters except
`/`
A double
`**`
matches any characters including
`/`
Question mark
`?`
matches only question mark
`?`
. If you want to match any character, use
`*`
instead.
Curly braces
`{}`
can be used to match a list of options separated by commas
`,`
Backslash
`\`
can be used to escape any of special characters (note to escape backslash itself as
`\\`
)

Examples:

`https://example.com/*.js`
matches
`https://example.com/file.js`
but not
`https://example.com/path/file.js`
`https://example.com/?page=1`
matches
`https://example.com/?page=1`

`https://example.com`
`**/*.js`
matches both
`https://example.com/file.js`
and
`https://example.com/path/file.js`
`**/*.{png,jpg,jpeg}`
matches all image requests

The glob pattern must match the entire URL, not just a part of it.

`**/*.{png,jpg,jpeg}`
matches all image requests

## Test timeout​ {#test-timeout}

Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

Timed out test produces the following error:


`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.`


Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

### Set test timeout in the config​ {#set-test-timeout-in-the-config}

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({timeout:120_000,});`


API reference:
testConfig.timeout (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-timeout)
.

You can set global timeout in the config.

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({globalTimeout:3_600_000,});`


API reference:
testConfig.globalTimeout (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-global-timeout)
.

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/auth>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

Details

Create
`tests/auth.setup.ts`

that will prepare authenticated browser state for all other tests.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

Create
`tests/auth.setup.ts`

To reliably issue the second mouse move, repeat your mouse.move() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-mouse#mouse-move) or locator.hover() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-hover) twice. llm_response:
To trigger the `dragover` event in all browsers, you need at least two mouse moves. Your current manual implementation is missing the second hover action.

To fix this, repeat the `locator.hover()` call on the drop element before releasing the mouse. The correct sequence is:

1. `await page.locator('#item-to-be-dragged').hover();`
2. `await page.mouse.down();`
3. `await page.locator('#item-to-drop-at').hover();`
4. `await page.locator('#item-to-drop-at').hover();` (The second hover)
5. `await page.mouse.up();`

**Alternative Approaches:**
*   **Recommended:** Use the built-in `locator.dragTo()` method, which handles the sequence of mouse actions (hover, press, move, release) automatically.
    ```javascript
    await page.locator('#item-to-be-dragged').dragTo(page.locator('#item-to-drop-at'));
    ```
*   **Alternative:** Use `page.dragAndDrop(source, target)`, which also performs the move, mousedown, move, and mouseup sequence.

CI killed our nightly job and left a report that looks like this. What confuses me is that no individual test failed or timed out — 486 passed, the rest were skipped, and the summary line is about the run rather than any one spec.

Running 1000 tests using 10 workers
  514 skipped
  486 passed
  Timed out waiting 3600s for the entire test run

I've been through the config and I can't find where 3600 is set — I certainly didn't write it. What is this limit and where does it come from?
reference: That message is the cap on the entire run, not a single test. Playwright ships without one, but you can set globalTimeout in the config (e.g. 3_600_000 for an hour) to stop a broken run from burning resources.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test supports a timeout for the whole test run. This prevents excess resource usage when everything went wrong. There is no default global timeout, but you can set a reasonable one in the config, for example one hour. Global timeout produces the following error:

Running 1000 tests using 10 workers

  514 skipped
  486 passed
  Timed out waiting 3600s for the entire test run

## Test timeout​ {#test-timeout}

Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

Timed out test produces the following error:


`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.`


Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between
`0`
and
`workers - 1`

`parallelIndex`
and a new
`workerIndex`
.

You can read an index from environment variables

and

are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

user_input:
My click fails because a hover overlay intercepts the click at the action point, even though I know the element is fine. Code:

await page.getByRole('button').click(); // fails actionability / receives-events

How can I bypass the check?
reference: Actionability checks include the element receiving pointer events; an overlay intercepting the click causes failure. If you know this is happening, bypass the checks with force: true, e.g. await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true }).
reference_contexts: Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability) checks and force the click:
await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });

Some actions like locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) support force option that disables non-essential actionability checks, for example passing truthy force to locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) method will not check that the target element actually receives click events.
llm_response:
To bypass the actionability checks when a hover overlay intercepts your click, you can use the `force` option within the `locator.click()` method.

Use the following code:

```javascript
await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });
```

This approach is recommended when you know that an overlay is intercepting the click, as it forces the action by bypassing the standard actionability checks (such as the check that ensures the element is not obscured by other elements).

Alternatively, if you want to simulate the click by any means possible without testing under real conditions, you can use `locator.dispatchEvent()` to trigger a programmatic DOM event:

```javascript
await page.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');
```

This method bypasses Playwright's actionability checks entirely and is equivalent to calling the standard Web API `HTMLElement.click()`.

Your XPath locator does not work because XPath does not pierce shadow roots.

While Playwright locators generally work with elements in the Shadow DOM by default, this is a specific exception. To resolve this, you should use a different locator strategy that is supported for Shadow DOM, such as:

*   **User-visible locators:** Prefer locators like `getByRole`, `getByText`, or `getByTestId`, which are recommended over XPath and CSS because they are less tied to implementation details and less likely to break.
*   **CSS selectors:** If you must use a selector-based approach, CSS selectors are supported and do pierce open shadow DOM.

For example, instead of your current XPath, you could use:
`await page.getByTestId('inner-details').click();` 
or 
`await page.locator('css=#inner-details').click();`

### Test Isolation​ {#test-isolation}

Playwright Test is based on the concept of
test fixtures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures)
such as the
built in page fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#built-in-fixtures)
, which is passed into your test. Pages are
isolated between tests due to the Browser Context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
, which is equivalent to a brand new browser profile. Every test gets a fresh environment, even when multiple tests run in a single browser.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('example test',async({page})=>{// "page" belongs to an isolated BrowserContext, created for this specific test.});test('another test',async({page})=>{// "page" in this second test is completely isolated from the first test.});`


### Using Test Hooks​ {#using-test-hooks}

You can use various
test hooks (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test)
such as
`test.describe`
to declare a group of tests and
`test

.beforeEach`
and
`test.afterEach`
which are executed before/after each test. Other hooks include the
`test.beforeAll`
and
`test.afterAll`
which are executed once per worker before/after all tests.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('navigation',()=>{test.beforeEach(async({page})=>{// Go to the starting url before each test.awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev/');});test('main navigation',async({page})=>{// Assertions use the expect API.awaitexpect(page).toHaveURL('https://playwright.dev/');});});`

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test is an end-to-end test framework for modern web apps. It bundles test runner, assertions, isolation, parallelization and rich tooling. Playwright supports Chromium, WebKit

and Firefox on Windows, Linux and macOS, locally or in CI, headless or headed, with native mobile emulation for Chrome (Android) and Mobile Safari.

How to open the HTML test report (https://playwright.dev/docs/intro#html-test-reports)

`preload.js`
file that contains the mock.

Next, add init script to the page.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';importpathfrom'path';test.beforeEach(async({page})=>{// Add script for every test in the beforeEach hook.// Make sure to correctly resolve the script path.awaitpage.addInitScript({path:path.resolve(__dirname,'../mocks/preload.js')});});`

page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api

Our submit-confirmation test fails maybe one run in ten on CI and never on my machine. When it fails the value read back is an empty string rather than the wrong string, so it looks like we're reading too early — but there's already a visibility check above this line, so the element is definitely on the page by the time we get here.

Adding a fixed wait makes it pass, which I know is the wrong answer. What's the right one?
reference: You're using a non-retrying check on asynchronously-updated content. Use a web-first auto-retrying assertion that waits until the condition is met, e.g. await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted'). It re-fetches and re-checks until it passes or the timeout is reached.
reference_contexts: Playwright also includes web-specific async matchers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions) that will wait until the expected condition is met. Consider the following example:
await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');

Playwright will be re-testing the element with the test id of status until the fetched element has the "Submitted" text. It will re-fetch the element and check it over and over, until the condition is met or until the timeout is reached.
llm_response:
The right approach is to replace your current code with an auto-retrying web-first assertion.

Instead of reading the text into a variable and then asserting on that variable, use `expect(locator).toHaveText()` directly. This method is engineered to reduce flakiness by automatically re-fetching the element and re-testing its content until the condition is met or the timeout is reached.

Replace your existing lines with this:

```javascript
await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');
```

**Why this is the right answer:**
*   **Auto-retrying:** Unlike reading the text into a variable (which captures the state at a single point in time), `expect(locator).toHaveText()` will continue to re-fetch the element and check its text content until it matches "Submitted" or the timeout (default 5 seconds) is reached.
*   **Web-first:** This is the recommended approach in the documentation to ensure test stability and avoid flakiness caused by asynchronous UI updates.
*   **Avoids manual waits:** This eliminates the need for fixed waits, which are discouraged.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given
`timeout`
, action fails with the
`TimeoutError`
.

For example, for
locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click)
, Playwright will ensure that:

locator resolves to exactly one element
element is
Visible (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#visible)
element is
Stable (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#stable)
, as in not animating or completed animation
element
Receives Events (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#receives-events)
, as in not obscured by other elements
element is
Enabled (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#enabled)

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

### Running Sequence​ {#running-sequence}

When working with tests that have a dependency, the dependency will always run first and once all tests from this project have passed, then the other projects will run in parallel.

Running order:

Tests in the 'setup' project run. Once all tests from this project have passed, then the tests from the dependent projects will start running.
Tests in the

'chromium', 'webkit' and 'firefox' projects run together. By default, these projects will
run in parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
, subject to the maximum workers limit.

If there are more than one dependency then these project dependencies will be run first and in parallel. If the tests from a dependency fails then the tests that rely on this project will not be run.

Tests in the 'Browser Login' and 'DataBase' projects run in parallel:
'Browser Login' passes
❌ 'DataBase' fails!

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called

### Live editing locators​ {#live-editing-locators}

### Picking locators​ {#picking-locators}

While debugging, you might need to choose a more resilient locator. You can do this by clicking on the
Pick Locator
button and hovering over any element in the browser window. While hovering over an element you will see the code needed to locate this element highlighted below. Clicking an element in the browser will add the locator into the field where you can then either tweak it or copy it into your code.

Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing
role, text and test id locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
. If Playwright finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient and uniquely identify the target element, so you don't have to worry about failing tests due to locators.

If actionability can't be reached, it will show the action as pending.

locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click)

### Picking locators​ {#picking-locators}

While debugging, you might need to choose a more resilient locator. You can do this by clicking on the
Pick Locator
button and hovering over any element in the browser window. While hovering over an element you will see the code needed to locate this element highlighted below. Clicking an element in the browser will add the locator into the field where you can then either tweak it or copy it into your code.

Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing
role, text and test id locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)

# Timeouts | Playwright

## Test timeout​ {#test-timeout}

Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

Timed out test produces the following error:


`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.`


Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and

user_input: A test keeps flaking on CI and I can't reproduce it locally. I want a way to see exactly what happened when it failed, without slowing down the whole run. What should I enable?
reference: Enable tracing on the first retry (trace: 'on-first-retry' with retries enabled). This produces a trace.zip for retried tests that you can open in Trace Viewer to explore each action, DOM snapshots, console and network. Traces are great for debugging failures on CI.
reference_contexts: Traces are a great way for debugging your tests when they fail on CI. You can open traces locally or in your browser on trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev) .

Traces should be run on continuous integration on the first retry of a failed test by setting the trace: 'on-first-retry' option in the test configuration file. This will produce a trace.zip file for each test that was retried.
llm_response:
To see exactly what happened when a test fails on CI without slowing down the whole run, you should enable **tracing** with the `trace: 'on-first-retry'` option in your `playwright.config.ts` file.

This configuration is recommended for CI environments because it only records a trace when a test fails and is retried, minimizing performance impact compared to recording traces for every test.

### How to enable it
Add the following to your `playwright.config.ts`:

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
});
```

### Alternative options
If you need different behavior, the `trace` option supports several other modes:
*   **`'retain-on-failure'`**: Records a trace for every test but removes it if the test passes. This is useful if you do not enable retries but still want traces for failed tests.
*   **`'retain-on-failure-and-retries'`**: Records a trace for each test run and retains all traces when an attempt fails, which is useful for comparing a passing trace with a failing one from a flaky test.
*   **`'on'`**: Records a trace for every test. This is **not recommended** as it is performance-heavy.

### How to analyze the failure
Once the trace is recorded, it is stored as a `trace.zip` file in the `test-results` directory. You can inspect it using the **Trace Viewer**, a GUI tool that provides a detailed timeline, DOM snapshots, network monitoring, and execution steps to help you diagnose the root cause of the failure. You can open the trace by:
1.  Clicking the trace icon in the generated **HTML Report**.
2.  Using the command line: `npx playwright show-report` or `npx playwright trace <path-to-trace.zip>`.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

## Failures​ {#failures}

Playwright Test runs tests in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Consider the following snippet:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('suite',()=>{test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});

test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});});`


When
all tests pass
, they will run in order in the same worker process.

Worker process starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
passes
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

Should
any test fail
, Playwright Test will discard the entire worker process along with the browser and will start a new one. Testing will continue in the new worker process starting`second flaky`
is retried and passes
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

This scheme works perfectly for independent tests and guarantees that failing tests can't affect healthy ones.

## Retries​ {#retries}

Playwright supports
test retries
. When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.


`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`


You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Give failing tests  second flaky2passed(4s)`


You can detect retries at runtime with
testInfo.retry (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#

test-info-retry)
, which is accessible to any test, hook or fixture. Here is an example that clears some server-side state before a retry.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('my test',async({page},testInfo)=>{if(testInfo.retry)awaitcleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();// ...});`


You can specify retries for a specific group of tests or a single file with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe(()=>{// All tests in this describe group will get 2 retry attempts.test.describe.configure({retries:2});test('test 1',async({page})=>{// ...});test('test 2',async({page})=>{// ...});});`


## Serial mode​ {#serial-mode}

Use
test.describe.serial() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-serial)
to group dependent tests to ensure they will always run together and in order. If one of the tests fails, all subsequent tests are skipped. All tests in the group are retried together.

Consider the following snippet that uses
`test.describe.serial`
:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'serial'});test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first

good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


When running without
retries (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#retries)
, all tests after the failure are skipped:

Worker process #1:
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`third good`
is skipped entirely

When running with
retries (https://playwright.dev/docs2:
`beforeAll`
hook runs again
`first good`
passes again
`second flaky`
passes
`third good`
passes

note
It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be efficiently run and retried independently.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

## Failures​ {#failures}

Playwright Test runs tests in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Consider the following snippet:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('suite',()=>{test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});
138|test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});});`


When
all tests pass
, they will run in order in the same worker process.

Worker process starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
passes
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

Should
any test fail
, Playwright Test will discard the entire worker process along with the browser and will start a new one. Testing will continue in the new worker process starting`second flaky`
is retried and passes
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

This scheme works perfectly for independent tests and guarantees that failing tests can't affect healthy ones.

## Retries​ {#retries}

Playwright supports
test retries
. When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.


`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`


You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Give failing tests  second flaky2passed(4s)`


You can detect retries at runtime with
testInfo.retry (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#
138|test-info-retry)
, which is accessible to any test, hook or fixture. Here is an example that clears some server-side state before a retry.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('my test',async({page},testInfo)=>{if(testInfo.retry)awaitcleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();// ...});`


You can specify retries for a specific group of tests or a single file with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe(()=>{// All tests in this describe group will get 2 retry attempts.test.describe.configure({retries:2});test('test 1',async({page})=>{// ...});test('test 2',async({page})=>{// ...});});`


## Serial mode​ {#serial-mode}

Use
test.describe.serial() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-serial)
to group dependent tests to ensure they will always run together and in order. If one of the tests fails, all subsequent tests are skipped. All tests in the group are retried together.

Consider the following snippet that uses
`test.describe.serial`
:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'serial'});test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first
138| good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


When running without
retries (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#retries)
, all tests after the failure are skipped:

Worker process #1:
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`third good`
is skipped entirely

When running with
retries (https://playwright.dev/docs2:
`beforeAll`
hook runs again
`first good`
passes again
`second flaky`
passes
`third good`
passes

note
It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be efficiently run and retried independently.

You can perform API testing directly within the Playwright framework without using a browser by utilizing the `APIRequestContext` class. Because Playwright is a comprehensive framework that includes a dedicated Node.js test runner, these API tests can run in the same command and be included in the same reports as your browser-based tests.

To implement this, you do not need to stand up a second framework. You can use the `APIRequestContext` class to monitor and modify HTTP, HTTPS, and WebSocket traffic. 

Key points regarding this approach:
*   **Integrated Execution:** Since Playwright's test runner supports project-based configuration, you can organize your API tests alongside your browser tests. They will execute in the same command and appear in the same HTML report.
*   **Network Capabilities:** The framework provides extensive capabilities for network interception and manipulation using the `Route` and `APIResponse` classes, in addition to `APIRequestContext`.
*   **Configuration:** You can manage your API testing requirements (such as base URLs and headers) within your existing `playwright.config.ts` file. For example, you can set `extraHTTPHeaders` or `httpCredentials` globally to apply to your requests.

user_input: Our dashboard greets people with 'Good morning' or 'Good evening' and stamps every row with a relative label like 'posted 3 hours ago'. The assertions on both pass when I run them at my desk and fail on the nightly build, which is obviously about when the run happens rather than the code. How do I make the page's idea of the current time deterministic?
reference: Pin the clock rather than trying to write assertions that hold at any hour. The recommended tool is page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')), which fixes what Date.now() and new Date() return so the greeting and the relative timestamps render the same way on every run. You can call it again mid-test to move to another fixed instant and re-assert. Reach for clock.install() only if the page's timers actually need time to progress — install is the heavier option that additionally lets you pauseAt, fastForward, runFor and resume — and setSystemTime is for advanced cases only.
reference_contexts: setFixedTime: Sets the fixed time for Date.now() and new Date().

The recommended approach is to use setFixedTime to set the time to a specific value. If that doesn't work for your use case, you can use install which allows you to pause time later on, fast forward it, tick it, etc. setSystemTime is only recommended for advanced use cases.
await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')); await page.goto('http://localhost:3333'); await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:00 AM');
llm_response:
To make the page's idea of the current time deterministic, you should use the Playwright **Clock** API.

The documentation recommends the following approaches:

1.  **`setFixedTime` (Recommended):** Use this method if you only need to test with a predefined time. It sets a fixed time for `Date.now()` and `new Date()` while keeping timers running.
    *   **Usage:** `await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00'));`

2.  **`install` (For advanced scenarios):** If `setFixedTime` does not meet your needs (e.g., you need to pause time, fast forward, or tick through it manually), use `install`.
    *   **Usage:** `await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2024-02-02T08:00:00') });`
    *   **Important:** You must call `install` before navigating to the page and before any other clock-related calls to avoid undefined behavior.

**Additional control methods available after `install`:**
*   **`pauseAt`:** Pauses the flow of time at a specific date and time.
    *   *Example:* `await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00'));`
*   **`fastForward`:** Advances the clock by a specific duration (e.g., `'05:00'` for five minutes).
*   **`runFor`:** Ticks through time manually, firing all timers and animation frames.

For best results, install the clock before navigating the page and set it to a time slightly before your intended test time to ensure timers function normally during the page loading process.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

A project is logical group of tests running with the same configuration. We use projects so we can run tests on different browsers and devices. Projects are configured in the
`playwright.config.ts`
file and once configured you can then run your tests on all projects or only on a specific project. You can also use projects to run the same tests in different configurations. For example, you can run the same tests in a logged-in and logged-out state.

By setting up projects you can also run a group of tests with different timeouts or retries or a group of tests against different environments such as staging and production, splitting tests per package/functionality and more.

user_input: I want Playwright to launch my dev server before tests locally, but on CI I want it to fail if the server isn't already handled. Actually — I just want it to reuse an already-running server locally but always start fresh on CI. How?
reference: Set reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI in the webServer config. Locally it reuses an already-running dev server; on CI it will not reuse and starts the server fresh.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a webServer option in the config file which gives you the ability to launch a local dev server before running your tests. This is ideal for when writing your tests during development and when you don't have a staging or production url to test against.

webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    stdout: 'ignore',
    stderr: 'pipe',
  },

If you're using Playwright's
Code Generator (https://playwright.dev/docs/codegen)
, generating aria snapshots is streamlined with its interactive interface:

"Assert snapshot" Action
: In the code generator, you can use the "Assert snapshot" action to automatically create a snapshot assertion for the selected elements. This is a quick way to capture the aria snapshot as part of your recorded test flow.
"Aria snapshot" Tab
: The "Aria snapshot" tab within the code generator interface visually represents the aria snapshot for a selected locator, letting you explore, inspect, and verify element roles, attributes, and accessible names to aid snapshot creation and review.

### Updating snapshots with@playwright/testand the--update-snapshotsflag​ {#updating-snapshots-with-playwrighttest-and-the---update-snapshots-flag}

When using the Playwright test runner (
`@playwright/test`
), you can automatically update snapshots with the
`--update-snapshots`
flag,
`-u`
for short.

Running tests with the
`--update-snapshots`
flag will update snapshots that did not match. Matching snapshots will not be updated.


`npx playwrighttest--update-snapshots`


Updating snapshots is useful when application structure changes require new snapshots as a baseline. Note that Playwright will wait for the maximum expect timeout specified in the test runner configuration to ensure the page is

Note that Playwright will wait for the maximum expect timeout specified in the test runner configuration to ensure the page is settled before taking the snapshot. It might be necessary to adjust the
`--timeout`
if the test hits the timeout while generating snapshots.

#### Snapshot patch files​ {#snapshot-patch-files}

When updating snapshots, Playwright creates patch files that capture differences. These patch files can be reviewed, applied, and committed to source control, allowing teams to track structural changes over time and ensure updates are consistent with application requirements.

The way source code is updated can be changed using the
`--update-source-method`
flag. There are several options available:

"patch"
(default): Generates a unified diff file that can be applied to the source code using
`git apply`
.
"3way"
: Generates merge conflict markers in your source code, allowing you to choose whether to accept changes.
"overwrite"
: Overwrites the source code with the new snapshot values.


`npx playwrighttest--update-snapshots --update-source-method=3way`

`toMatchAriaSnapshot`

`name`

file extension.

Methods

All tests run by the worker reuse the same user.

## Shard tests between multiple machines​ {#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines}

Playwright Test can shard a test suite, so that it can be executed on multiple machines. See
sharding guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding)

`npx playwrighttest--shard=2/3`


## Limit failures and fail fast​ {#limit-failures-and-fail-fast}

You can limit the number of failed tests in the whole test suite by setting
`maxFailures`
config option or passing
`--max-failures`
command line flag.

When running with "max failures" set, Playwright Test will stop after reaching this number of failed tests and skip any tests that were not executed yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on broken test suites.

Passing command line option:


`npx playwrighttest--max-failures=10`


Setting in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

## Worker index and parallel index​ {#worker-index-and-parallel-index}

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between
`0`
and
`workers - 1`
. When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same
`parallelIndex`
and a new
`workerIndex`
.

You can read an index from environment variables
`process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX`
and
`process.env.TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX`
, or access them through
testInfo.workerIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-worker-index)
and
testInfo.parallelIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-parallel-index)
.

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes

are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

All tests run in worker processes. These processes
0| are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

user_input: Our stack needs two processes up before anything can be tested — the web front end and a separate API service — and the API one is slow, usually a minute and a half before it answers. Right now the run gives up and everything fails at the first navigation. How should this be configured?
reference: The `webServer` option accepts an array, so declare both processes and let the runner wait for each one. Give each entry a `command`, a `url` to poll for readiness, a `name` so failures are attributable, and — for the slow one — a `timeout` big enough to cover the boot, e.g. `timeout: 120 * 1000`, since the default is not enough for a server that takes 90 seconds. Setting `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` on each keeps local iteration fast while forcing a fresh boot on CI. Pair it with `use: { baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000' }` so specs can navigate with relative paths.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a webServer option in the config file which gives you the ability to launch a local dev server before running your tests.
Webservers can sometimes take longer to boot up. In this case, you can increase the timeout to wait for the server to start.

webServer: [ { command: 'npm run start', url: 'http://localhost:3000', name: 'Frontend', timeout: 120 * 1000, reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI, }, { command: 'npm run backend', url: 'http://localhost:3333', name: 'Backend', timeout: 120 * 1000, reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI, } ]

user_input: My CSS selectors keep breaking every time the DOM changes. I want locators that survive refactors. What should I use instead?
reference: Prefer user-facing locators like role and text (getByRole, getByText) or an explicit test id contract (getByTestId) instead of CSS/XPath, which are tied to implementation and break when the DOM changes.
reference_contexts: CSS and XPath are not recommended as the DOM can often change leading to non resilient tests. Instead, try to come up with a locator that is close to how the user perceives the page such as role locators or define an explicit testing contract using test ids.
Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass.
llm_response:
To create more resilient locators that survive refactors, you should avoid CSS selectors and XPath, as they are often tied to the DOM structure or implementation and break when the page changes.

Instead, you should use locators that reflect how a user perceives the page. The documentation recommends the following approaches:

*   **User-facing attributes:** Use locators that are close to the user's perspective, such as **role locators** (e.g., `getByRole`) or **accessible labels** (e.g., `getByLabel`, `getByPlaceholder`, `getByAltText`).
*   **Test IDs:** Define an explicit testing contract using **test IDs** (e.g., `data-testid`).

Additionally, you can use the `LOCATOR.NORMALIZE` method, which is designed to optimize element referencing by converting a locator to follow these industry best practices, prioritizing user-facing attributes and test IDs over traditional CSS selectors.

worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures)
fixture has its own timeout, equal to the test timeout. You can change the timeout for a worker-scoped fixture in the same way.

user_input: I keep writing teardown code to clear cookies and local storage so one spec doesn't poison the next, and it still isn't enough — things like already-visited link styling survive anyway, and a test that fails halfway never gets to its cleanup. I'd rather every test just began from nothing.
reference: That's the default, and cleaning up between tests is the strategy the docs advise against — it's easy to forget, and some state (visited links being the standard example) simply cannot be cleaned up, so leakage shows up later as a confusing failure in a different test. The alternative is to start from scratch, which is what browser contexts give you: each test gets its own BrowserContext, an incognito-like profile with its own cookies, local storage and session storage, created fresh for that test and completely isolated even when several run in one browser. With the test runner this happens automatically — the `page` and `context` fixtures in each test belong to a context created for it — so you can delete the teardown rather than fix it. Contexts are cheap and fast to create, so there's no cost argument for reusing one.
reference_contexts: Tests written with Playwright execute in isolated clean-slate environments called browser contexts. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures.

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using BrowserContexts which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. They are fast and cheap to create and are completely isolated, even when running in a single browser.

There are two different strategies when it comes to Test Isolation: start from scratch or cleanup in between. The problem with cleaning up in between tests is that it can be easy to forget to clean up and some things are impossible to clean up such as "visited links".
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.

## Option 2: Configure globalSetup and globalTeardown​ {#option-2-configure-globalsetup-and-globalteardown}

You can use the
`globalSetup`
option in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration#advanced-configuration)
to set something up once before running all tests. The global setup file must export a single function that takes a config object. This function will be run once before all the tests.

Similarly, use
`globalTeardown`
to run something once after all the tests. Alternatively, let
`globalSetup`
return a function that will be used as a global teardown. You can pass data such as port number, authentication tokens, etc. from your global setup to your tests using environment variables.

note
Beware that
`globalSetup`
and
`globalTeardown`
lack some features — see the
intro (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-global-setup-teardown#introduction)

user_input: I set a geolocation for my test, but partway through I need to move the user to a different location. Can I change geolocation mid-test?
reference: Yes — call context.setGeolocation() mid-test to move the user. Just remember the change is context-wide: it affects every page in that context, not one page in isolation.
reference_contexts: Note you can only change geolocation for all pages in the context.

## Opening the HTML report​ {#opening-the-html-report}

The HTML report shows you a report of all your tests that have been run and on which browsers as well as how long they took. Tests can be filtered by passed tests, failed, flaky, or skipped tests. You can also search for a particular test. Clicking on a test opens the detailed view where you can see more information on your tests such as the errors, the test steps, and the trace.


`npx playwright show-report`


## Opening the trace​ {#opening-the-trace}

In the HTML report, click on the trace icon next to the test file name to directly open the trace for the required test.

You can also click to open the detailed view of the test and scroll down to the
`'Traces'`
tab and open the trace by clicking on the trace screenshot.

To learn more about reporters, check out our detailed guide on reporters including the
HTML Reporter (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#html-reporter)
.

## Viewing the trace​ {#viewing-the-trace}

View traces of your test by clicking through each action or hovering using the timeline and see the state of the page before and after the action. Inspect the log, source and network, errors, and console during each step of the test. The trace viewer creates a DOM snapshot so

you can fully interact with it and open the browser DevTools to inspect the HTML, CSS, etc.

To learn more about traces, check out our detailed guide on
Trace Viewer (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer)
.

## Opening the HTML report​ {#opening-the-html-report}

The HTML report shows you a report of all your tests that have been run and on which browsers as well as how long they took. Tests can be filtered by passed tests, failed, flaky, or skipped tests. You can also search for a particular test. Clicking on a test opens the detailed view where you can see more information on your tests such as the errors, the test steps, and the trace.


`npx playwright show-report`


## Opening the trace​ {#opening-the-trace}

In the HTML report, click on the trace icon next to the test file name to directly open the trace for the required test.

You can also click to open the detailed view of the test and scroll down to the
`'Traces'`
tab and open the trace by clicking on the trace screenshot.

To learn more about reporters, check out our detailed guide on reporters including the
HTML Reporter (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#html-reporter)
.

user_input: I run sharded tests as separate CI jobs and end up with a separate report per shard. I want one combined report at the end. What's the workflow?
reference: Use the blob reporter on CI, upload each shard's blob report as an artifact, then in a final job download all blob reports into one directory and run npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html to produce a single combined HTML report.
reference_contexts: In the previous example, each test shard has its own test report. If you want to have a combined report showing all the test results from all the shards, you can merge them.
To merge reports from multiple shards, put the blob report files into a single directory, for example all-blob-reports . Blob report names contain shard number, so they will not clash.
npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
llm_response:
To combine reports from multiple sharded CI jobs into a single HTML report, follow these steps:

### 1. Configure the Blob Reporter
In your `playwright.config.ts`, set the reporter to `blob` when running in CI. This generates binary `.zip` files containing test results and attachments for each shard.

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
});
```

### 2. Collect Blob Reports
After your sharded test jobs complete, you must collect the generated blob reports from each job into a single directory (e.g., `all-blob-reports`). 

If using **GitHub Actions**, you can achieve this by:
*   Uploading the `blob-report` directory as an artifact in your test jobs.
*   Using `actions/download-artifact` in a subsequent "merge" job to download all blob reports into a single folder (e.g., `all-blob-reports`).

### 3. Merge the Reports
Once all blob reports are in one directory, run the `merge-reports` CLI command to generate the final unified HTML report:

```bash
npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
```

This command processes the files in the specified directory and outputs a standard HTML report into the `playwright-report` directory. You can then upload this directory as an artifact to view the combined results.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

## Balancing Shards​ {#balancing-shards}

Sharding can be done at two levels of granularity depending on whether you use the
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
option or not. This affects how the tests are balanced across the shards.

## Merging reports from multiple shards​ {#merging-reports-from-multiple-shards}

In the previous example, each test shard has its own test report. If you want to have a combined report showing all the test results from all the shards, you can merge them.

Start with adding
`blob`
reporter to the config when running on CI:

playwright.config.ts

`exportdefaultdefineConfig({testDir:'./tests',reporter:process.env.CI?'blob':'html',});`


Blob report contains information about all the tests that were run and their results as well as all test attachments such as traces and screenshot diffs. Blob reports can be merged and converted to any other Playwright report. By default, blob report will be generated into
`blob-report`
directory. You can learn about
blob report options here (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#blob-reporter)
.

To merge reports from multiple shards, put the blob report files into a single directory, for example
`all-blob-reports`
. Blob report names contain shard number, so they will not clash.

Afterwards, run
`npx playwright merge-reports`
command:


`npx playwright merge-reports--reporterhtml ./all-blob-reports`


This will produce a standard HTML report into
`playwright-report`
directory.

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its

## Why is Test Isolation Important?​ {#why-is-test-isolation-important}

No failure carry-over. If one test fails it doesn't affect the other test.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
option or not. This affects how the tests are balanced across the shards.

`blob-report`
directory. You can learn about

.

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

### Generating Tests with CodeGen​ {#generating-tests-with-codegen}

CodeGen is Playwright's powerful test generation tool that automatically creates test code by recording your interactions with a web page. Instead of writing tests from scratch, you can simply navigate through your application while CodeGen captures your actions and converts them into reliable test code with proper locators and assertions.

Record a New Test
: Click
Record new
in the sidebar. A browser window will open. As you interact with the page, Playwright will automatically generate the test code. You can also generate assertions from the recording toolbar.

Record at Cursor
: Place your cursor inside an existing test and click
Record at cursor
to add new actions at that specific point.
Pick a Locator
: Use the
Pick locator
tool to click on any element in the opened browser. Playwright will determine the best locator and copy it to your clipboard, ready to be pasted into your code.

To learn more, see our
CodeGen guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/codegen)
.

# Evaluating JavaScript | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/evaluating>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright scripts run in your Playwright environment. Your page scripts run in the browser page environment. Those environments don't intersect, they are running in different virtual machines in different processes and even potentially on different computers.

The
page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
API can run a JavaScript function in the context of the web page and bring results back to the Playwright environment. Browser globals like
`window`
and
`document`
can be used in
`evaluate`
.


`consthref=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>document.location.href);`


If the result is a Promise or if the function is asynchronous evaluate will automatically wait until it's resolved:


`conststatus=awaitpage.evaluate(async()=>{constresponse=awaitfetch(location.href);returnresponse.status;});`


## Different environments​ {#different-environments}

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing

environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

The following snippet is
WRONG
because it uses the variable directly:


`constdata='some data';constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>{// WRONG: there is no "data" in the web page.window.myApp.use(data);});`


The following snippet is
CORRECT
because it passes the value explicitly as an argument:


`constdata='some data';// Pass |data| as a parameter.constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(data=>{window.myApp.use(data);},data);`


## Evaluation Argument​ {#evaluation-argument}

Playwright evaluation methods like
page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
take a single optional argument. This argument can be a mix of
Serializable (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify#Description)
values and
JSHandle (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-jshandle)

### Generating Tests with CodeGen​ {#generating-tests-with-codegen}

CodeGen is Playwright's powerful test generation tool that automatically creates test code by recording your interactions with a web page. Instead of writing tests from scratch, you can simply navigate through your application while CodeGen captures your actions and converts them into reliable test code with proper locators and assertions.

Record a New Test
: Click
Record new
in the sidebar. A browser window will open. As you interact with the page, Playwright will automatically generate the test code. You can also generate assertions from the recording toolbar.

Record at Cursor
: Place your cursor inside an existing test and click
Record at cursor
to add new actions at that specific point.
Pick a Locator
: Use the
Pick locator
tool to click on any element in the opened browser. Playwright will determine the best locator and copy it to your clipboard, ready to be pasted into your code.

To learn more, see our
CodeGen guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/codegen)
.

<https://playwright.dev/docs/evaluating>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright scripts run in your Playwright environment. Your page scripts run in the browser page environment. Those environments don't intersect, they are running in different virtual machines in different processes and even potentially on different computers.

The
page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
API can run a JavaScript function in the context of the web page and bring results back to the Playwright environment. Browser globals like
`window`
and
`document`
can be used in
`evaluate`
.


`consthref=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>document.location.href);`


If the result is a Promise or if the function is asynchronous evaluate will automatically wait until it's resolved:


`conststatus=awaitpage.evaluate(async()=>{constresponse=awaitfetch(location.href);returnresponse.status;});`


## Different environments​ {#different-environments}

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing
281| environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

The following snippet is
WRONG
because it uses the variable directly:


`constdata='some data';constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>{// WRONG: there is no "data" in the web page.window.myApp.use(data);});`


The following snippet is
CORRECT
because it passes the value explicitly as an argument:


`constdata='some data';// Pass |data| as a parameter.constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(data=>{window.myApp.use(data);},data);`


## Evaluation Argument​ {#evaluation-argument}

Playwright evaluation methods like
page.evaluate() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-evaluate)
take a single optional argument. This argument can be a mix of

## Why is Test Isolation Important?​ {#why-is-test-isolation-important}

No failure carry-over. If one test fails it doesn't affect the other test.
Easy to debug errors or flakiness, because you can run just a single test as many times as you'd like.
